It simply defaults to domination by whichever agents are most willing to coerce. Neutrality is not the absence of enforcement; it is the enforcement of the conditions under which choice remains possible. Nor does the framework pretend to a clean decision procedure that classifies every policy — monopoly, redistribution, regulation, collective risk — as constitutive or outcome-imposing. Under dynamic agency no such procedure exists, and the indeterminacy is not a flaw; it is a consequence of governing evolving agents under uncertainty. Political contestation persists. What changes is the constraint: contestation itself must not collapse into domination. Utopia in Motion The sophisticated utopian no longer proposes a final state. He proposes a direction. Civilization, on this view, is a system to be steered: define adaptiveness, measure it, and optimize over time. Robin Hanson gives the position its most disciplined form.[^hanson-rationality] Civilization has elevated abstract reasoning without grounding it in adaptiveness, producing cultural drift and institutional decay; from this he derives a trilemma — abandon rationality and return to tradition, continue with half-measures and accept collapse, or commit fully to stronger, explicitly adaptive rational steering. His pessimism follows naturally: if rationality is our steering mechanism and we refuse to use it decisively, decline is the default. [^hanson-rationality]: Robin Hanson, “Rationality: Quit, All In, Or Bust,” Overcoming Bias , https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/rationality-quit-all-in-or-bust. The diagnosis identifies a real pressure. The conclusion misidentifies its source. The failure is not that rationality has been insufficiently empowered; it is that rationality has been assigned a role it cannot coherently play. Hanson's argument rests on the premise that civilization constitutes a system with a well-defined objective function, such that adaptiveness can be specified, measured, and optimized. Accept that premise and the rest is nearly tautological: steering requires goals, goals require metrics, metrics require tradeoffs, and rationality is conscripted to justify the tradeoffs. But civilization is not an agent, not a unified optimizer, and not a system whose futures can be ranked without remainder. It is a plurality of agents with divergent values inhabiting futures that are not commensurable in aggregate. Treating that plurality as a single optimization problem is the same category error as the static utopia, committed before any discussion of metrics begins. The assumption that civilization must be steered at all already presupposes the mechanism that produces collapse. Civilizational optimization is utopia in dynamic form. And the dynamic form inherits the static form's cost structure. Any attempt to steer requires a scalar ranking of outcomes — a function that collapses complex, multidimensional world-states into a single ordering so that some futures can be declared preferable. That collapse is not a modeling convenience; it is the defining act of optimization. Because agent-relative outcomes cannot be injected into a single scalar without loss, some dimensions must be ignored, discounted, or overridden. Once optimization pressure is applied, any gradient that rewards harm becomes instrumentally valuable: the system learns that reducing some agents' degrees of freedom improves its objective, and the reduction ceases to be accidental. It becomes structural. Refining the metric does not eliminate the sacrifice; it increases its efficiency. It is tempting to exempt survival — to treat "civilization must survive" as an axiom rather than a metric. The temptation is mistaken. Survival is already an aggregate claim that presupposes a privileged description of which civilization, in which form, at whose expense. A binary constraint differs from a scalar metric only in smoothness, not in authorization, and there is no stable stopping point between "must survive" and "must maximize." Survival enforced by coercion across non-consenting agents preserves continuity at the cost of agency, and what persists under those conditions is no longer the thing it claims to protect. The usual rejoinder invokes Moloch: multipolar traps and competitive spirals prove that steering is unavoidable. This reverses the causal arrow. Moloch is not an external adversary that pluralistic systems must defeat; he is a diagnostic signature of systems that aggregate agents without consent and then apply outcome pressure across the aggregation — coordination attempted through outcome metrics rather than action constraints, losses justified by global pressure, exit subordinated to performance. Intensifying civilizational steering to defeat Moloch reinstates the mechanism that generates him. The same reversal applies to the drift Hanson blames on reason: rationality does not steer societies — institutions do, incentive structures do, power gradients do. Leviathan does not emerge because people reason too much. It emerges because centralized systems discover that suppressing choice improves their metrics, and nothing in their architecture forbids acting on the discovery. Rationality is not the engine of that process; it is the tool conscripted to rationalize it. So the trilemma dissolves. There is no option to abandon rationality, because reasoning is not a discretionary cultural fashion. There is no coherent way to commit fully to steering without authorizing sacrifice. And collapse is not the consequence of insufficient optimization but of excessive closure — the progressive elimination of exit, dissent, and local autonomy in service of aggregate goals. The missing option is structural restraint: coordination through constraints on action — rules governing interaction, boundaries, liability, and exit — never constraints on outcomes, which collapse plural futures into a single acceptable set and authorize enforcement when agents diverge. The moment outcome-constraints are enforced, even in binary form, optimization has already begun. Within this discipline rationality keeps an indispensable but sharply negative role: enforcing consistency, exposing illicit aggregations, detecting sacrifice gradients, auditing governance rules — preventing incoherent architectures from stabilizing. It supplies no direction, purpose, or destiny, which makes it anti-utopian by construction. Two admissions keep this honest. First, nothing guarantees that every large-scale coordination problem admits an agency-preserving solution; some may be insoluble under these constraints, and insolubility carries real costs — it just does not license coercive outcome control. Second, a civilization that refuses to convert its members into instruments may be outcompeted by one that does not. That is not an oversight. It is the cost of treating agency as constitutive rather than optional. Agents may still collectively accept extraordinary constraints under explicit, bounded emergencies — the optimization pressure behind arguments for steering against existential risk makes those moments genuinely hard. What is forbidden is the conversion of emergency into entitlement: emergency powers without revocation, contestability, and exit are not temporary deviations but civilizational phase transitions. A system that preserves itself by abolishing agency has not solved the problem of survival. It has changed the subject. The Sacrifice Pattern Static closure and dynamic optimization share a risk already developed in Volume IV: a system can improve its measured performance by pushing unmeasured costs onto agents with weak standing. Intent is not enough to detect the failure. The useful audit asks who loses reachable futures, whether that loss is doing work for the objective, whether affected agents can contest the measurement, and whether the system can revise without suppressing exit or feedback. This is a risk condition, not a theorem that every aggregate metric or institution is a sacrifice engine. Measurement can surface hidden harms as well as conceal them; coordination can protect vulnerable agents as well as consume them. The danger rises when objectives are narrow, per-agent effects are hidden, responsibility is diffuse, and those bearing the cost lack voice or exit. The corresponding safeguards — explicit accountability, disaggregated impact, constraints on coercion, contestability, and review — are stated formally in Agency Conservation and the Sacrifice Pattern and developed in Governance Without Gods. This chapter needs only the political consequence: no promised endpoint may exempt itself from that audit. After Closure The egalitarian temptation ends here, at its logical terminus: the arrangement final enough that no one may revise it. That destination does not exist. Not because human nature is too crooked for it — the argument concedes nothing to cynicism — but because value, once recognized as agent-relative, cannot be frozen without dissolving the agency that gives value its meaning. Heterogeneous agents do not compose into an authoritative optimum; arrangements claiming finality must defend themselves against drift with machinery that substitutes administration for choice; systems that optimize under standing asymmetry learn to eat their components, slowly at first, then systematically. So the central question of political design changes shape. It is no longer which world deserves to be called perfect but which architectures can host ongoing revision while resisting the domination patterns that erase agency itself — no global objectives, no aggregate metrics, no authorized sacrifice, no closure of futures. That is a question about structure, not aspiration, and it sets the agenda for what follows: why governance at scale destroys the very evaluability steering presupposes is where The Limits of Leviathan begins, and the temperament that refuses closure under uncertainty and irreversibility is the discipline of Centrism as a Discipline. Utopia promised an end to politics. What remains, once the promise is withdrawn, is the harder and more interesting problem: order without an endpoint.

title: The Authoritarian Default
subtitle: Psychology, dynamics, definition
volume: Volume 7 — Liberty, Coercion, and Governance
content: Consider the shape of human political history from a height. Sumer crowned god-kings. Egypt deified its pharaohs. China ruled by the mandate of heaven, Rome by the divinity of emperors, medieval Europe by the divine right of kings; the Aztecs, the Inca, the Khmer, the Ottomans, the politburos of the twentieth century — very different societies repeatedly produced authority concentrated above, submission expected below, and dissent treated as disease. The recurrence is broad, though neither every society nor every period fits one design. The liberal package defended here — individual authorship, authority answerable to the governed, criticism protected against decree — appeared late and incompletely as a durable institutional combination, though practices of consent, dispersed authority, resistance, and deliberation are older and wider. Liberal orders require maintenance; authoritarian recovery after collapse is a recurrent risk, not a law that erases counterexamples. A recurrence that broad demands explanations at more than one altitude. Institutions, material conditions, war, technology, and particular ideologies matter; so may psychological tendencies that travel across them. The hypothesis of this chapter is that authoritarian coordination often comes cheaply, exploiting ready cognitive and social responses, while liberal order is a precious, fragile achievement that has to be built and maintained. Default names that recurrent risk, not a universal state installed identically in every person or culture. The Instinct for Submission Six forces, supported at different levels and interacting differently across populations and institutions, can converge on the same output. They are recurring human susceptibilities rather than defects unique to one group. Hierarchy sometimes paid. Humans evolved in varied small-group environments where coordination under scarcity and threat could reward rapid deference as well as deliberation, coalition-building, and resistance to bad leaders. One plausible contribution to present psychology is therefore a mix of biological and cultural selection for context-sensitive hierarchy: under perceived danger, closing ranks can be locally advantageous. That is a hypothesis about recurring pressures, not a finding that efficient hierarchies universally outlasted deliberative groups or that evolution optimized a single objective called group survival. The narrower inheritance is enough for this argument: threat can make submission feel protective rather than alien. Thinking is expensive, and outsourcing it is cheap. Autonomous agency demands constant vigilance, cognitive effort, and emotional resilience — every decision owned, every belief audited. Human cognition economizes with heuristics, and the grandest heuristic of all is authority: accept the prescribed beliefs and norms, and an enormous portion of life's decisions are precomputed. The savings are real, and they grow with stress. In uncertain or threatening environments, when cognitive resources are most taxed, the shortcut becomes most attractive — which is precisely when authoritarians come recruiting. Conformity polices the group from inside. Conformity bias and in-group favoritism run deep. In many ancestral environments, exclusion carried severe costs, so aligning with majority opinion or authority could protect access to cooperation and survival. Authoritarianism can leverage those tendencies rather than create them from nothing. Rigid conformity can strengthen cohesion, make internal disagreement costly, and simplify social interaction into a test with one approved answer. Certainty is a consumer good. People often seek epistemic security — clear, comforting, unequivocal accounts of the world — and recoil from ambiguity. Authoritarian narratives can sell exactly this: absolute truth, fixed moral clarity, an answer for everything. The alternative defended here — that interpreted claims depend on conditions open to re-examination — is demanding. Under stress, comfortable certainty can outsell accurate uncertainty. Dogma has some of candy's advantage over medicine. Fear is easily weaponized. A credible coercive threat exploits the deepest aversion an organism has. Faced with it, submission is at first a calculation, then a habit, and finally something worse: internalized, so that the subject polices himself and calls it loyalty. This is the self-reinforcing dynamic that lets authoritarian systems economize on enforcement — the fear does most of the work, and after enough time the fear is no longer even experienced as fear. Agency is a burden as well as a good. Autonomy entails continuous personal accountability, and the weight of it — every outcome traceable to one's own choices — can be crushing. By centralizing agency in a figure or an institution, authoritarianism relieves the individual of responsibility for his own life. Every abdication is also an acquittal: whatever happens next is no longer your fault. The trade is emotionally appealing and ethically ruinous, and it is offered fresh every day. Put the six together and notice what they share: each can discount part of the cost of being an agent. Hierarchy discounts coordination, authority discounts thought, conformity discounts conflict, dogma discounts doubt, submission discounts fear, and abdication discounts responsibility. Authoritarianism need not be an alien imposition on human psychology; under some conditions it can become a path of less resistance, a point missed by theories that treat tyranny only as something done to populations. A strongman can be met partway by followers whose needs his offer fits like a key. Nor does the pattern require a strongman at all: the same psychology, operating at low intensity through ordinary institutions, can supply the willing personnel of The Censorship Machine — no commissars needed, just people choosing certainty and safety one referral at a time. At full dose, submission helped make the regimes anatomized in Against Communism administrable alongside violence, surveillance, patronage, and ideology. The practical inversion follows. Liberal, autonomous, critically rational life cannot be treated as a condition that maintains itself. It is a cultural and institutional project that must be re-argued, re-taught, and re-defended against recurrent pressures. The work does not become obsolete merely because one generation built safeguards. The Cycle If the pull is recurrent, it should be visible inside liberal orders too — not only as coups, but as a pattern in ordinary politics. One testable version is that political actors have stronger incentives to champion liberal constraints when out of power than when those constraints limit them in office. The mechanism is that the principles are held instrumentally. To a faction out of power, universal liberal values — free speech, individual autonomy, tolerance — are the best tools available. They build the broadest possible coalitions, win public sympathy, and indict incumbents by standards the incumbents profess. But the moment the faction gains authority, its priorities shift from coalition-building to coalition-maintenance, and the same values change sign. Free speech now protects the opposition. Tolerance now shelters the rival. Limited government now limits us . Principles that were load-bearing on the way up become obstacles at the top — because they were rented for the climb, never owned. The risk crosses factions, and that symmetry is diagnostic. Parts of the left have abandoned free expression while holding institutional power, rationalizing censorship as necessary combat against harmful and dangerous ideas. Parts of the right have abandoned limited-government commitments when dominant, citing social stability or national security. Each side can document the other's betrayal while experiencing its own as an unfortunate necessity. Fear supplies the emergency, certainty supplies the justification, and conformity supplies the applause. Weaponized fear needs an enemy, and an opponent's real excesses can supply one. Notice what the rule buys you: a forecasting question. Betrayals need not arrive at random; transitions into power change the costs of tolerating opposition. That recurrent incentive makes a movement's manifesto weak evidence by itself about behavior in office. A stronger forecast reads both commitments and incentives: ask what professed values will cost once the coalition holding them becomes the governing one. The observer who catalogues the other side's betrayals while trusting his own side's promises has still misunderstood the risk — the incentive is not a fact about them . That is the equilibrium a society risks when the cycle runs unopposed: competing authoritarianisms, each justifying its abuses by citing its opponents' excesses. Each faction's overreach becomes the other's recruiting poster; each round of retaliation licenses the next; and the contest stops being between liberty and control and becomes a contest over whose control. The machinery need not reverse itself merely because its costs become visible; actors can remain locally responsive to incentives that sustain it. What interrupts the ratchet is a different kind of actor. Principled behavior — upholding the same values in power and out of it, regardless of short-term advantage — is inherently costly. It means sacrificing expediency, enduring discomfort, and tolerating dissent one has the means to silence. Because it is costly, it is rare; because the cycle cannot be broken any other way, it is indispensable. Principled actors are what make a liberal order more than a truce between authoritarianisms waiting for their turn: they stabilize expectations, reduce the transactional friction of politics, and keep norms of accountability and transparency alive by observing them when observation hurts. Breaking the authoritarian cycle requires valuing liberal principles as terminal goals — things held for their own sake — and not as instrumental tactics. What that commitment looks like as a working discipline of governance is the subject of Centrism as a Discipline. Three Axes Andrew Doyle has argued[^doyle-default] that authoritarianism is humanity's default state, and that liberalism is not truly an ideology at all but the absence of ideological dogmatism — a method for negotiating our flawed and uncertain condition. This chapter defends a bounded version of the first claim: recurring pressures can make authoritarian coordination cheaper unless institutions resist them. The second half is nearly right, and getting it exactly right requires saying what the two orientations actually disagree about. The opposition runs along three axes. [^doyle-default]: Andrew Doyle, discussion of liberalism and authoritarianism, YouTube, https://youtu.be/4Ohmspi6T-E?list=PLRdTugBInz19PmwsPhMjrzABr7yPUl1ry. Authority versus autonomy. Authoritarianism centralizes decision-making in hierarchical authorities — political, cultural, or religious — and demands submission and conformity toward them. Liberalism takes individual autonomy as foundational: agents own their own lives, and self-determination is not a means to some further political end but the end itself. Coercion versus consent. The authoritarian project inherently runs on coercion; the credible threat of harm is not a regrettable last resort but the ordinary instrument of rule. Liberalism inverts the burden: it treats every act of coercion as standing in need of justification, and builds its institutions on voluntary consent and negotiation instead. It does not pretend coercion can be abolished outright — the conditions under which it survives the justification test are the business of The Grey Zone — but it insists that coercion is always the thing on trial, never the judge. Dogmatic certainty versus conditional epistemology. Authoritarianism insists its truths are fixed, immutable, and non-negotiable. Liberalism is epistemically humble: truths are conditional, context-dependent, and permanently subject to scrutiny and revision. This third axis is the deepest, because the other two follow from it. If your doctrine is infallible, then dissent is simply error, error has no rights, and coercion in truth's service is a favor to its victims. If instead all truth is conditional, then you need institutions that keep revision possible — free speech to surface criticism, consent to register values, revocable authority to correct mistakes. The politics falls out of the epistemology. State the axes that starkly and an objection arrives on schedule: liberal societies also want order. They have laws, police, courts, hierarchies of their own. Doesn't everyone want stability? Yes — and the shared goal is precisely where the distinction sharpens rather than blurs. Both orientations aim at social coordination. Authoritarianism treats top-down coercion and overridden agency as ordinary instruments; liberalism places coercion under continuing justification and builds more heavily through consent, reciprocity, and rights. Order is not the differentiator. The technology and burden of proof for producing it are. The same clarification disposes of law. Authoritarian states have law in abundance — rule by law, the statute as an instrument of power, binding subjects but never rulers, applied arbitrarily and read most creatively against enemies. Liberal societies uphold rule of law: a universal constraint, uniform, predictable, and impartial, that limits even — especially — those in power. The presence of a legal code tells you nothing about which order you are living in. The test is whether the code binds the men who wrote it. So Doyle's formulation can be sharpened. Liberalism is not merely an absence of dogmatism, as if it were defined by what it lacks. It is the political embodiment of a definite epistemic position: that human knowledge is fallible, that every truth is conditional, and that a decent political order must therefore be built to survive being wrong — criticism legal, authority revocable, cooperation voluntary. That is not the absence of conviction. It is a conviction about human fallibility, held firmly enough to build institutions around, and it is what makes liberalism uniquely suited to navigating an uncertain world without surrendering autonomy or reaching for the whip. The picture, assembled: a default and a discipline. The default is the cheaper recurrent risk — six tendencies that institutions can amplify, restrain, or redirect, and that factions in power have incentives to exploit. The discipline must be learned, argued for, and paid for by every generation, and its rarest and most essential input is people who hold its principles when holding them hurts. That much helps explain why liberalism is often embattled. It does not yet explain why liberal institutions can forfeit constituencies to ideologies with worse records and better stories. That is the subject of Why Liberalism Loses.

title: Why Liberalism Loses
subtitle: The structural unpopularity of liberty
volume: Volume 7 — Liberty, Coercion, and Governance
content: Classical liberalism has one of the strangest track records in the history of ideas: it seems to win every experiment and lose every election. The metaphor overstates the science — history runs no controlled experiment that isolates liberal institutions from geography, state capacity, culture, security, and policy — but the pattern it points at is real. Individual liberty, open exchange, constrained government, and impartial law are associated with many rich, free, and creative societies, and the contrasts between South and North Korea or West and East Berlin remain powerful evidence, not the whole causal proof. Its institutions can win the comparison while its philosophy loses the constituency. Yet explicit classical liberalism remains chronically unpopular and on the defensive even among many beneficiaries. Its gains are easily absorbed as background conditions while its principles remain available for attack. The Authoritarian Default proposed half of this puzzle: authoritarian movements can exploit recurrent tendencies toward hierarchy, conformity, tribal loyalty, and certainty, while liberal safeguards require continuing maintenance. I will not restate that psychology here. This chapter is about the other half: disadvantages specific to liberalism's message and institutions. Understanding those handicaps is the difference between a diagnosis and a grievance, and I intend this chapter as the former. Start with the position, because caricatures do much of the losing. Classical liberalism joins individual moral primacy, voluntary exchange, limited government, impartial law, property, pluralism, and the recognition that complex cooperation can emerge without a designer. Each has been argued elsewhere in this volume. The question here is why the package is so hard to sell. The Structural Handicaps Spontaneous order is counterintuitive. Human cognition seeks intentionality behind complex phenomena. A god, king, or conspiracy satisfies; an equilibrium of millions of uncoordinated decisions does not. The claim that beneficial order arises without centralized control therefore reads as mysterious or suspicious. When prices rise, someone must be gouging; when shortage appears, someone must be hoarding. The idea that no one is steering, and that this is why the system works, is among the least intuitive true propositions ever discovered. Liberalism's foundational insight is a permanent marketing liability. Its benefits are dispersed; the grievances against it are concentrated. Markets lower many prices a little, continuously and invisibly. A tariff, subsidy, or license gives an identifiable group a large visible benefit. Liberty's gains are counterfactual careers and goods kept cheap by competition; nobody marches in gratitude for those. Concentrated beneficiaries organize while the diffuse majority paying stays home. Politics rewards centralizers. Visible intervention pays in prestige, influence, and the appearance of action. "I passed a program" is a slogan; "I declined to interfere" is not. Restraint creates no monument, ribbon-cutting, or grateful constituency. Liberalism asks officeholders to win power and not use it — roughly asking sharks to veganism — which is why later chapters seek structural answers rather than better sharks. Democracy discounts the future. Benefits arrive before the next election and concentrate on the grateful; distorted incentives, debt, and institutional decay arrive later and diffusely. Trading invisible future harm for visible present help responds rationally to the scoreboard. Liberal payoffs compound slowly and repeatedly lose to that discount rate. The fixed-pie fallacy biases every audience. If wealth is a pile rather than a process, every fortune is theft and every disparity an indictment. Wealth Is Not a Pile owns the economics; the political consequence is that redistribution looks like common sense and markets like a rigged casino. Every demagogue knows how to play the zero-sum intuition. The egalitarian instinct recoils from visible inequality. Liberalism insists on equality before the law and refuses to promise equality of outcomes — and humans instinctively read unequal outcomes as evidence of injustice. The inference from disparity to injury is invalid, as I argued in Against Envy, but it is emotionally automatic, which makes liberal policy permanently vulnerable to the charge of coldness. The rival who promises to close the gap will always sound kinder than the one who explains why the gap is not itself a wound. Narratives want heroes. Founders, monarchs, liberators, and revolutionaries make stories; anonymous entrepreneurs, incremental innovators, contract, and custom make poor protagonists. There is no statue of the unknown shopkeeper. A philosophy of emergent order concedes the narrative field to ideologies offering saviors and, when things go wrong, scapegoats. It refuses to run a machine of its own. Liberalism resists indoctrination because manufacturing believers would betray its premises. Rivals freely recruit through tribal appeal, parties, youth wings, catechisms, and belonging. Liberalism fields individual arguers against organized movements. The tribal pull is chapter 23's subject; the irony here is that liberalism is under-provisioned with advocates because it practices what it preaches. These handicaps compound where collectivist traditions are stronger, liberal institutions thinner, and authoritarian rule more familiar. The philosophy travels badly for the same reasons it polls badly at home. That is the catalogue. Notice what it adds up to: not a conspiracy against liberty and not a run of bad luck, but a systematic mismatch between what liberalism is and what political competition rewards. The next question is what it loses to — and the answer is not, usually, tyranny. It is something far more comfortable. The Political Triangle The familiar left–right spectrum obscures more than it reveals; I return to the poverty of that binary in Words That Lost Their Teeth. A better map for present purposes is a triangle whose vertices are three pure answers to the question of what government is for: Vertex Offers Characteristic goods --- --- --- Individualism Self-determination Sovereignty, responsibility, accountability Maternalism Care Welfare, support, the social safety net Paternalism Order Warfare, law and order, protection Each vertex has an honest appeal. Individualism offers freedom to shape and own a life. Maternalism offers protection from hardship and market volatility. Paternalism offers regulation, policing, defense, and stability. Mainstream politics contests the triangle's lower half: the left leans maternal, the right paternal, and both bid for the center. The individualist apex is claimed by everyone and pursued by no one because concentrated interests, centralizing incentives, electoral discounting, and hunger for protectors pull downward. Liberal democracies settle near the center: enough autonomy to generate wealth, welfare to blunt hardship, and order to keep streets calm. The equilibrium is genuinely stable, which is exactly the problem. Permanent Adolescence The center shelters citizens enough to foster dependence, protects them enough to limit accountability, and regulates them enough to discourage risk. No single policy does this; the equilibrium does. Each maternal program removes a hardship and a reason to build resilience. Each paternal rule removes a danger and a decision once owned by the citizen. Individualism keeps the machine productive while responsibility is optimized away from both directions. The result is permanent adolescence. The adolescent has real freedoms and constraints, someone to feed him and someone to ground him, but no point at which the full weight of life lands on his shoulders. The triangle's center institutionalizes that condition as citizenship: passive beneficiaries become consumers of governance rather than accountable agents. The equilibrium may be pragmatically optimal in the short run. It wins by offering visible care, visible protection, and enough freedom to finance both. It is self-reinforcing: citizens formed by dependency demand more of it. This is the ratchet in The Authoritarian Default: crisis moves the equilibrium away from the apex while each sheltered cohort shrinks the constituency for moving back. Liberalism loses to a comfortable arrangement that dissolves its constituency one reasonable protection at a time. Losing by One's Own Hand Structural handicaps are not an alibi. When a party selects standard-bearers primarily by identity criteria rather than demonstrated competence and broad appeal, voters read tokenism or pandering. When insiders anoint a candidate rather than submit the choice to open competition, the candidacy begins with a legitimacy deficit. Both abandon liberalism's own discovery procedure: competition over who deserves to win. A movement that suspends it internally while praising it publicly should expect voters to notice. That is the diagnostic frame for everything in this chapter. Liberalism's unpopularity is real, structural, and traceable: a philosophy that is subtle, abstract, and intellectually demanding, competing against rivals engineered for the evolved palate. It offers no myths, no scapegoats, no saviors — only the difficult and unglamorous challenge of self-responsibility, intellectual rigor, and tolerance. Naming the handicaps is not an excuse for losing to them. A position that keeps losing winnable arguments has more to learn than to lament, and the burden falls on those of us who hold it: to make spontaneous order visible, to give dispersed benefits a voice, to build institutions that do not depend on politicians restraining themselves — the project of the rest of this volume — and to remember that a philosophy of adulthood cannot win by promising comfort. It can only win by producing adults who no longer want to be governed like children.

title: Fictions of the Collective
subtitle: National interests are interpretations, not primitives
volume: Volume 7 — Liberty, Coercion, and Governance
content: "The 'realist' view of international affairs is false. People don't, and can't, act in their interests because they don't know what those are until they have a world view." — David Deutsch[^deutsch-interests] [^deutsch-interests]: David Deutsch (@DavidDeutschOxf), post on X, January 2026, https://x.com/DavidDeutschOxf/status/2007808783662084219. Few phrases in politics carry as much moral authority while concealing as much conceptual confusion as national interest . It appears in speeches just before wars begin, in memoranda authorizing surveillance, in arguments for secrecy, sacrifice, and coercion. It is spoken with the cadence of inevitability, as though it names a hard constraint imposed by reality itself. That cadence is doing almost all the work. The Individualist Premise identified the category error of attributing mental states and moral standing to abstractions. "National interest" and "collective will" cash that error out politically, converting group reification into a license to compel members and disabling the mechanisms that could expose a mistaken policy. Two errors stack: interests are treated as objective facts waiting to be read off the world, and a nation as the kind of thing that can possess them. They fail independently. Interests Are Not Primitives An interest presupposes an explanatory framework: a model of the world, causal theory, evaluation of outcomes, assessment of risk, and time horizon. Actors fail not only by irrational pursuit but by misidentifying their interests through a false worldview. Political realism treats interests as fixed inputs; they are outputs — conclusions of fallible theories wearing the costume of premises. Acknowledging this does not require denying hard constraints. Annihilation is incompatible with continued agency. Suffocation is incompatible with life. There are physical and biological limits that no worldview can negotiate away. But constraints are not interests. They rule out futures without selecting among the remaining ones. The moment a society moves from "we cannot survive this" to "therefore we must do that ," it has crossed from physics into interpretation — and interpretation is fallible. Physics never issues policy. It closes doors; it does not tell you which of the open ones to walk through. Every "therefore" in a national-security argument is supplied by a theory, and theories can be wrong. Interests are therefore conjectures about which actions produce futures an actor would endorse. Knowledge grows through conjecture exposed to criticism, not by reading certainty off the world (Rationality Without Foundations). Talk of interests is useful while contestable, revisable, and answerable to outcomes. Trouble begins when a conjecture becomes a command. Nations Are Not Agents A nation has no unified belief state, value function, or vantage. It is a changing aggregate of individuals, institutions, incentives, traditions, and power relations, often in conflict. Treating that pattern as a chooser is an analytical convenience; national interest silently converts the convenience into ontology and presents erased individual agency as collective rationality. This critique is not aimed at shorthand. Historians and analysts who write "Britain sought to contain France" are compressing a pattern of individual decisions, filtered through institutions that amplified some voices and silenced others, and the compression can be useful. The critique is aimed at the elevation of "national interest" from analytical device to justificatory principle — where uncertainty may be acknowledged rhetorically but is erased operationally, and one faction's judgment is enforced on everyone as necessity. That elevation is what gives the concept its political potency, and it is exactly the move The Individualist Premise called the compression becoming a lie. The Vanishing Intersection Could aggregation rescue the idea? Sean Carroll defines government as "the organized expression of our collective will,"[^carroll-government] the instrument of society's shared priorities. [^carroll-government]: Sean Carroll, “AMA June 2025,” Mindscape podcast, June 2, 2025, https://www.preposterousuniverse.com/podcast/2025/06/02/ama-june-2025/. Define that will operationally as the intersection of preferences held by every member. Small, intimate groups may share enough experience and tradition for the intersection to have content. Scale up and the intersection shrinks: every member is another chance for a preference to be absent, while differences in upbringing, priorities, and belief magnify divergence. At city or national scale it approaches empty. The standard reply is that the collective will operates at the level of abstract values rather than particular preferences — surely everyone wants "fairness," "freedom," "prosperity," "security." But this agreement is superficial, and it fractures the instant it touches policy. Everyone endorses fairness until fairness must be cashed out as a tax schedule; everyone endorses security until security must be cashed out as a surveillance program, a conscription order, a war. The abstract word gathers unanimous assent precisely because each person fills it with his own theory of what it requires — theories that contradict each other at every concrete decision point. Consensus on the syllables is not consensus on anything a government can do. At governance scale, government expresses majority, elite, or institutional preferences under rhetorical cover. "Collective will" borrows the standing of unanimous consent for decisions lacking it. This does not settle when governance is justified — The Grey Zone does that — but it prevents the phrase from making coercion disappear. How the Fallacy Licenses Harm The phrase endures because its indeterminacy is useful: power can fill it, and necessity shields it from reply. Once policy becomes national interest, a hypothesis becomes a requirement. Disagreement is moralized: a rival model becomes disloyalty to a will already declared. A judgment defended as necessity handles criticism by reclassifying the critic. The claim also becomes unfalsifiable. Disaster becomes unavoidable sacrifice, insufficient resolve, or necessary cost. A framework in which no outcome counts against policy does not choose policies; it insulates them. Once this structure is in place, coercion ceases to be a regrettable last resort. It becomes a duty. Individuals are no longer agents whose judgments matter, but instruments whose compliance is required. Extreme harm no longer requires pathological actors; it requires only ordinary officials operating within a framework that has reclassified choice as necessity. This is why the strongest form of the fallacy always appears where the stakes are declared highest — above all in defense, where "the national interest" underwrites the claim that protection requires sovereignty, a claim The Hardest Case: Defense examines in full. The same structure reappears wherever safety is invoked to place some judgment beyond challenge — including, in our own moment, the politics of AI safety, where "alignment" quietly presupposes an agreed collective target that does not exist. Catastrophe as Epistemic Failure The historical record reflects this pattern with disturbing regularity. The most destructive regimes of the twentieth century did not collapse because they were insufficiently committed to their interests. They collapsed because they enforced false explanatory models, suppressed dissent, and thereby froze their own capacity for error correction. Once disagreement is criminalized, rational execution accelerates descent. Policy becomes more coherent, optimized, and catastrophic because its false model cannot be challenged. The state executes the plan faithfully; the plan executes the error faithfully. Censorship, propaganda, and punishment are symptoms of epistemic weakness: judgment defended by force because it cannot survive argument. Free speech, criticism, and contestable authority are the machinery by which civilization converts coercion into coordination. National-interest rhetoric switches that machinery off. Best Current Judgment, Not Destiny Leaders still must act under pressure and genuine uncertainty. Corrigibility is not paralysis, and action does not require pretending uncertainty has vanished. Planes fly before theories are complete; treatments proceed without certainty. Successful action remains open to criticism, reversal, and learning. National-interest language converts provisional commitment into dogma. Centrism as a Discipline owns the positive method of acting decisively while keeping correction possible. Political action shapes possible futures without knowing which will occur. National-interest claims collapse that uncertainty prematurely and enforce one account of which futures count, foreclosing alternatives as well as producing outcomes. Interests must remain conjectures rather than commands: contestable, revisable, and exposed to criticism. There is no national interest or collective will in the sense political rhetoric requires, only agents acting through imperfect models. Abandoning the fiction requires neither passivity nor indecision, only leaders willing to say: this is our best current judgment, not our destiny — and to remain answerable when it proves wrong. That is why some of the worst acts in history have been justified in its name — and why they will continue to be, as long as the fallacy goes unchallenged.

title: Words That Lost Their Teeth
subtitle: Semantic hygiene for political language
volume: Volume 7 — Liberty, Coercion, and Governance
content: Consider what the word "socialist" is asked to cover. It names the regime that built Auschwitz. It names the regime that built the Gulag. And it names the regime that built the Danish healthcare system. One word, stretched across an ethno-nationalist death cult, a class-revolutionary police state, and a prosperous parliamentary democracy where the trains run on time and nobody disappears in the night. A word that covers all three of those things conveys almost nothing. Whoever uses it unqualified is not making a claim; he is making a noise. "Fascist" has likewise eroded from ultranationalism, corporatist statism, militarism, and violent authoritarian control into "people I dislike on the right." The same wear has claimed "communist," "liberal," "neoliberal," and "far right." Instruments became gestures. This is more than pedantry. Political vocabulary is an instrument panel; gauges that always read the same leave judgment blind. A society unable to distinguish a Nazi from a social democrat in language will condemn the harmless and excuse the monstrous. The remedy is not new words. It is taxonomy plus discipline: split the inflated terms into the distinct things they name, then hold the line on usage. This chapter does that for the two worst offenders. Three Socialisms The word socialism has historically named three systems with different ideals, methods, and outcomes. National Socialism is ethno-nationalist authoritarianism. Nazi Germany appropriated worker and anti-capitalist language while subordinating freedom and economic rights to the nation-state and racial identity. Its economics were corporatist: private ownership on paper, state direction in fact. Oppression, violence, and genocide define its legacy. International Socialism — Marxist-Leninist communism — championed global working-class solidarity and abolition of private ownership. The Soviet Union and Maoist China centralized political and economic command, crushing individual rights in the name of class struggle. Its record is broadly discredited, though it retains Western admirers who never lived under it. Liberal Socialism — social democracy or welfare capitalism — keeps democratic government, individual rights, private ownership, and markets while adding regulation and social provision. Nordic countries, Canada, and much of Western Europe have made this model stable and durably popular. Set the three side by side and the differences stop being subtle: Aspect National Socialism International Socialism Liberal Socialism --- --- --- --- Central goal Ethnic-nationalist supremacy International proletarian solidarity Democratic individual and collective flourishing Economic control Corporatist authoritarianism Centrally planned economy Regulated market economy Individual freedom Severely restricted Severely restricted historically Protected and prioritized Democracy Explicitly anti-democratic Explicitly anti-democratic historically Explicitly democratic The Axis That Matters On the conventional axis, National and International Socialism are mortal opposites — far right and far left, enemies from Weimar's streets through the Eastern Front. Yet on every row measuring treatment of people, they converge: authoritarian government, suppressed rights, and state control. The rivalry was real; the resemblance is realer. Two prison camps do not become opposites because their flags differ. Liberal Socialism sits nearer International Socialism in its language of solidarity and redistribution, yet is the structural outlier: rights protected, democracy explicit, markets retained. The structural axis — how power is held and constrained — matters more than what power is nominally for. The first two systems name different beneficiaries, race and class, but share a total state, blocked exit, and punished dissent. The third shares some distributive goals while rejecting the machinery. Content divides the first two; structure unites them and separates both from Liberal Socialism. This is one of two complementary lenses this book applies to socialism: this chapter's taxonomy sorts regime types by structure, while the dose taxonomy of Against Socialism — dose, domain, monopoly, exit, feedback — measures how much of the socialist mechanism a system administers and how it is constrained; the two lenses answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other. And it is the same insight that the political triangle in Why Liberalism Loses encodes geometrically: the interesting divide in politics is not left versus right but the axis running orthogonal to it. Why Precision Matters Everybody knows Sweden is not the Soviet Union, but arguments run on words. A term binding three referents lets a conclusion proved about one travel silently to the others. Call a national healthcare proposal "socialism" and you have implied — without ever having to argue it — that it sits on a continuum ending in gulags. Call it that in front of an audience that associates the word with Denmark and you have implied it is obviously benign. Both moves are fraudulent, and both are ubiquitous. The defender of welfare capitalism gets saddled with Stalin's body count; the apologist for central planning hides behind Norwegian pension funds. Each equivocation is only possible because the word refuses to distinguish. The confusion compounds when inflated words collide: "The Nazis were socialists, so the left are the real fascists"; "Fascism is capitalism in decay, so the right are the real fascists." Terms baggy enough to hold any opponent prevent convergence because the parties no longer discuss the same object. Distinguishing the three socialisms is a precondition for arguing about them. Doyle's Razor "Fascist" is the most inflated label. When everyone is a fascist, the word means nothing and genuine fascists hide among the falsely accused. The writer Andrew Doyle has proposed a simple intervention, which I will call Doyle's razor: If you condone the murder of your political opponents, you're a fascist. This is not exhaustive — historical fascism includes more than political murder — but it is a sharp sufficient condition, cheap to check and indifferent to faction. The test earns its keep whenever political violence occurs. After a political assassination in a polarized society, the pattern is depressingly reliable: the great majority across the spectrum condemn the killing, while a fringe openly celebrates it — and screenshots of the celebrants circulate until they create the impression that a large fraction of the other side was cheering. That impression is exaggeration, and the exaggeration is itself a form of the inflation this chapter is against. What exists is a noisy fringe: individuals who crossed the line into condoning political murder. Doyle's razor preserves both judgments. The celebratory fringe are not their movement's mainstream, but cheering political bloodshed crosses the line. Fascism is not a neighbor who votes wrong or holds an unpopular opinion; here it is the legitimization of political murder, whatever banner covers it. Notice that the discourse around fascism suffers from two opposite distortions, and the razor slices through both: 1. Overuse. Calling every ordinary conservative — or every ordinary progressive — a fascist drains the term of meaning and slanders the innocent. 2. Under-focus. Ignoring the fringe that condones political violence leaves genuine fascism unnamed and uncontested. The errors reinforce each other. Overuse turns accusation into noise and gives the guilty cover; under-focus leaves them unnamed. Moral condemnation is currency: debase it and it buys nothing. Doyle's test preserves weight through precision. I should be clear about what this chapter is and is not claiming. The inflation of political labels is not always innocent drift; often it is deliberate — a weapon in memetic conflict, wielded to destroy reputations and forbid positions rather than describe them. The mechanics of that weaponization — how cancel culture deploys inflated labels as social artillery, and how algorithmic media corrupt language itself — belong to the next volume's treatment of narrative warfare. This chapter's business is the definitional hygiene that makes the weapon detectable: you cannot recognize a debased currency until you know what the coin was originally worth. A LARPitarian Interlude Semantic hygiene has a temperamental cousin: hold political identity lightly. Erving Goffman described social life as contextual performance, and political flags, team language, and ritual denunciations are often costume. Call the honest version LARPitarianism: everybody should be free to LARP; nobody should be forced to LARP. The first clause protects the right to adopt and discard roles, including ridiculous ones. The second forbids compulsory identities, rituals, and casting strangers as villains. Label inflation is forced LARP: a casting director nobody hired conscripts the public as extras. Retiring the Compressed Axes "Socialist," "fascist," and left–right all compress high-dimensional political arrangements into an epithet or line. The table shows the loss: structural twins land at opposite ends and structural opposites side by side. Equivocations and label warfare exploit that loss. Taxonomy and discipline are the repair this chapter can offer: split the words, publish the table, apply the razor. But the honest endpoint of the argument is that the compressed axes should not be repaired so much as retired. What politics actually needs is more dimensions, not better epithets — a way of locating political arrangements in the full space of their structural properties: how power is held, whether exit exists, what feedback constrains the rulers, how much of life the system claims. In that space, "how far left?" dissolves as a question, and the question that replaces it — is this arrangement inside or outside the region where agency remains viable? — turns out to be answerable. Building that space is the work of The Admissible Region. This chapter has only sharpened the old tools; that one replaces them.

title: Centrism as a Discipline
subtitle: Governance under uncertainty and irreversibility
volume: Volume 7 — Liberty, Coercion, and Governance
content: The last five chapters have been a pathology report. Utopian closure turns out to be a machine for degrading agency (Against Utopia). Authoritarian politics can exploit cheaper recurrent tendencies, while liberal safeguards demand maintenance (The Authoritarian Default). Liberalism carries structural messaging disadvantages even where its institutions perform well (Why Liberalism Loses). The collectives in whose name politics is conducted turn out not to exist as agents (Fictions of the Collective), and the vocabulary we would need to say any of this precisely turns out to have been inflated into noise (Words That Lost Their Teeth). The natural question is what survives the diagnosis. What does a political actor look like who has absorbed all of it — the pull toward submission, the fragility of liberal orders, the nonexistence of the collective chooser, the corruption of the words? What temperament is left standing? My answer is centrism. Centrism is usually treated as a punchline. From the left it is framed as moral cowardice; from the right it is dismissed as incoherence or surrender. In both cases it is portrayed as a lack of conviction rather than as a considered response to political reality. That framing misses what centrism is when taken seriously. I am not defending moderation as aesthetic balance, compromise as a virtue in itself, or neutrality as an end. I am defending centrism as a governance discipline shaped by three facts about political systems: they are complex, our knowledge of them is radically incomplete, and many of their failure modes are irreversible. Systems with those properties reward variance tolerance, institutional friction, and humility about outcomes. Centrism is what falls out once those constraints are treated as real rather than as rhetorical concessions. A Discipline, Not a Demographic The word "centrism" is usually used sociologically, to name a cluster of voters, parties, or elites — the people in the middle of the distribution, the ones who split the difference. That is not what I am defending. The demographic middle has no special claim to wisdom; the midpoint between two errors is usually a third error. And many self-described centrists act from inertia, donor capture, or simple risk aversion — triangulating between whatever the loudest factions currently demand. Those failures are real, and they belong to the practitioners. Centrism, as I mean it, is a discipline: a method for governing under uncertainty. Like any discipline, it can be practiced well or poorly, and failure to meet its standards indicts the agent rather than the framework — no one thinks a botched proof discredits mathematics. Treating centrism this way aligns it with the other load-bearing concepts of this philosophy: agency, coherence, survivability. What matters is not the label but adherence to the constraint. A politician who calls himself a radical while carefully bounding failure modes and preserving reversibility is practicing the discipline; a politician who calls himself a centrist while drifting wherever incumbency pulls him is not. The Shared Error of the Extremes Ideological extremes differ sharply in values, narratives, and policy goals, and they spend their energy advertising those differences. But they converge on a deeper structural assumption about what politics is . Politics is framed as a moral battlefield. Progress becomes victory. Opposition becomes enemy. Power becomes the mechanism through which righteousness is enforced. Once politics is framed this way, the pathologies follow with the predictability of a theorem. Tradeoffs lose legitimacy — on a battlefield, weighing costs against the cause is treason. Variance becomes injustice by default — any difference in outcomes is evidence of the enemy's work. Institutions appear as obstacles rather than safeguards, since anything that slows the righteous slows righteousness. And confidence in moral intent substitutes for analysis of consequences: the question "what will this do?" is displaced by the question "whose side are you on?" Centrism rejects the battlefield frame at the root. It treats politics as an ongoing coordination problem among agents with partially conflicting goals, incomplete information, and asymmetric power. In that setting, moral clarity does not dissolve complexity. It often amplifies error, because clarity licenses action, and action whose downstream effects are poorly understood does damage in proportion to the confidence behind it. The extremist's certainty is not a moral achievement layered on top of his analysis; it is a substitute for the analysis. Society as an Evolving Ecology Political metaphors are not decoration; they shape what actions seem permissible. The battlefield metaphor invites escalation. The mechanical metaphor — society as a machine with levers and dials — invites control fantasies, five-year plans, social engineering. A more accurate frame treats society as an evolving ecology of agents embedded in institutions. Ecological systems exhibit properties that matter politically. They contain multiple actors with divergent incentives, so no intervention lands on a passive substrate; everything is answered. They display path dependence: early changes constrain later options, and you cannot rerun the founding. They produce nonlinear cascades, where small interventions trigger disproportionate effects through channels no one mapped in advance. They settle into local equilibria rather than global optima — which is one more reason the utopian project is ill-typed: there is no summit to march to, only the landscape and its basins. And they accumulate irreversible losses alongside slow recoveries: an institution that took three generations to grow can be destroyed in a legislative season. Systems like this cannot be solved . They can be stewarded, stressed, or destroyed. Interventions do not simply produce outcomes; they alter selection pressures and reshape incentives, so the system that receives the tenth intervention is not the system that received the first. Success in such a system usually looks like resilience rather than perfection. Centrism aligns with this reality: governance becomes an exercise in damage control and coordination rather than moral purification. That description will strike the battlefield mind as a shameful lowering of ambition. It is actually the recognition of what kind of object a society is. The Variance Distinction The immediate objection is that this counsels acquiescence — that treating society as an ecology means shrugging at whatever the ecology produces. The answer to that objection is the moral compass of the whole discipline, and it turns on a distinction about variance. Variance appears wherever systems are allowed to operate. Differences in outcomes, capacities, preferences, and performance arise even under scrupulously fair rules, because agents differ and choices compound. Treating all variance as injustice therefore leads somewhere perverse: since variance cannot be eliminated, the political strategy becomes abolishing its measurement, punishing its visibility, or attributing all of it to malice — anything but understanding its causes. But it does not follow that all variance is acceptable. The crucial distinction separates variance produced by voluntary interaction from variance produced by coercive constraint. The former reflects decentralized choice under conditions of agency: people wanted different things, tried different things, and got different results. The latter reflects the systematic suppression of agency through credible threats of harm: people got different results because some of them were not permitted to choose. Centrism tolerates the first kind and treats the second as a structural defect requiring intervention. The question is never whether outcomes differ — they always will — but whether the differences arise from preserved agency or enforced constraint. Once that distinction is explicit, the standard accusation collapses. Tolerance is not complicity. It is selective intolerance of coercion: indifferent to divergence as such, implacable toward the boot. The Epistemic Core Centrism is an epistemic stance before it is a political one. Its premises are about knowledge, not values: knowledge is partial, incentives are complex, feedback is delayed, and error scales with power. A wrong idea held by a pamphleteer is a wrong idea; the same idea held by a ministry is a catastrophe. Several commitments follow. Intentions do not guarantee outcomes, so a policy's moral advertising is evidence of nothing. Second-order effects often dominate first-order gains, so the visible beneficiary is not the ledger. Policies should be judged by how they behave under stress — under bad administrators, adversarial gaming, and conditions their authors never imagined — not by how they sound in principle. And authority should be distributed and constrained, because confidence magnifies harm precisely when it is wrong, and it cannot announce in advance which time that will be. This posture is Conditionalism applied to politics. Political claims, like all claims, make sense only relative to background conditions: a policy that works in one institutional ecology fails in another, and an unconditional policy prescription is not strong but incoherent, because its effects depend on a context it refuses to specify. Centrism internalizes this and builds governance structures that expect revision rather than finality. It is the political face of error correction — and it explains why the fictions of the previous chapter are not innocent. A regime that claims to act for "the national interest" has not merely made a category error; it has disabled the machinery by which its errors could be named, because dissent from a fiction can always be moralized into disloyalty. Institutions as Scaffolding Institutions attract constant criticism for being slow, imperfect, and unjust, and the criticisms are frequently accurate. The mistake is in the implied standard. The function of institutions is not to instantiate moral truth. It is to constrain error and limit damage when judgment fails — and judgment always eventually fails. This is Hayek's insight about knowledge.[^hayek] No central authority can gather the dispersed, tacit, local information that a society runs on, so centralized control is not merely tyrannical but ignorant, and its confidence is exactly as dangerous as its reach. Institutions, on this view, encode lessons learned through failure — each procedural annoyance is usually the scar of some past disaster — and they create friction precisely where confidence would otherwise run unchecked. The independent court that blocks the popular measure, the supermajority requirement that stalls the urgent reform: these are not defects in the machinery of righteousness. They are the machinery working. [^hayek]: “Friedrich Hayek,” Wikipedia , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich Hayek. Centrism therefore treats institutions as ecological scaffolding, and reforms them the way one reforms scaffolding: to improve resilience and feedback, not to enforce ideological purity. The objective is survivability under stress rather than optimization under ideal assumptions. This is also why the centrist can never share the revolutionary's cheerful talk of demolition. The revolutionary sees an obstacle between the people and the good; the centrist sees a load-bearing wall between the people and the recurring disasters that built it. Metastable Evil Ecological stability, however, is not sufficient for legitimacy — and here the discipline diverges sharply from the conservatism it is often mistaken for. Some systems remain stable precisely by suppressing agency. Feudalism persisted for centuries. Caste systems persisted for millennia. Apartheid was internally coherent, administratively sophisticated, and brutally enforced. These were not equilibria in any honorable sense; they were metastable failure states — arrangements held in place not by the consent of their participants but by the systematic, credible threat of harm against anyone who moved. Under the centrist discipline, such systems qualify as defects, not as ecosystems to steward. The variance distinction does the work: what these systems stabilized was coercively produced variance, the exact thing the compass condemns. When a social order's stability depends on coercion and irreversible agency suppression, disruption becomes justified even at significant risk. Abolition, the civil rights movement, and decolonization required decisive rupture, because incrementalism, in those cases, was not prudence — it was the preservation of injustice on the installment plan. So centrism does not oppose disruption as such. It evaluates disruption the way it evaluates everything else: by its failure modes, and by whether it expands or destroys agency over time. The discipline that counsels patience with a flawed but correctable institution is the same discipline that licenses rupture against an incorrigible one. The two verdicts are not in tension; they are the same test applied to different facts. Selective Decisiveness The standing charge against centrism is passivity — that it is a philosophy of the fence, constitutionally incapable of action at the speed events demand. The record of the previous section already answers half of this. The other half is answered by how the discipline handles irreversibility. Centrism is selectively decisive. It supports strong action where failure modes are bounded and inaction produces irreversible loss. Existential risks — climate instability, uncontrolled AI deployment, demographic collapse, institutional failure — are precisely the cases where the discipline demands nonlinear response, because "wait and see" is itself a bet, and against an irreversible downside it is a bad one. What centrism opposes is not decisive action but a particular justification for it: moral certainty in place of analysis of failure dynamics. The activist who demands sweeping power because the cause is righteous and the activist who demands it because he has mapped the failure modes and bounded them are asking for the same thing on entirely different warrants, and only one of them should get it. How badly this goes when the battlefield frame captures a genuine risk domain — when "safety" becomes a permission layer for installing one faction's values — is a story told elsewhere in this book. The discipline is the same across every domain. Act where delay compounds harm. Constrain power where certainty outruns knowledge. Preserve reversibility where possible. Accept irreversibility only where every alternative collapses the future entirely. Why Centrism Provokes Hostility If centrism is this — a compass, a set of tests, a licensed capacity for rupture — why is it despised from both directions? The polemical answer is that it is despised for what it denies. Extremes depend on narrative clarity. They require villains, heroes, and historical destiny; the story is not an ornament on the politics but its fuel. Centrism denies every faction its moral monopoly. It treats opponents as constrained agents rather than embodiments of evil, which spoils the villain role. It treats institutions as safety devices rather than as sacred obstacles or disposable tools, which spoils the plot. Above all, it refuses to convert conviction into entitlement — to accept that the intensity of a belief confers any right to enforce it. For movements built on identity and certainty, this refusal is experienced as an attack, and the resulting hostility reflects psychological loss as much as political disagreement. Centrism takes away the story people were living inside. There is an aesthetic version of the same complaint: centrism is boring. It offers no catharsis and no final victory, and this is taken as evidence of weakness. A different interpretation fits the evidence better. Systems that endure optimize for continuity and error correction rather than drama. The politics that keeps societies functioning rarely trends, because it does not satisfy narrative hunger; the sewage system does not inspire anthems either. Extremism compresses complexity into moral slogans — that is its product, and the compression is why it travels. Centrism refuses compression, and pays for the refusal in reach. Boredom, here, is not the absence of a position. It is what a position sounds like when it declines to lie about how complicated things are. Principled Actors A discipline is only as real as its practitioners, and this returns us to where Part VI began. The authoritarian cycle described at the opening of this part runs on instrumental principle: factions champion free speech, tolerance, and limited government while out of power, because universal principles build coalitions, and abandon them upon gaining power, because the same principles then obstruct. Both left and right run the cycle on schedule. What breaks the cycle is not a better constitution but a rarer kind of agent. Genuinely principled behavior — upholding values regardless of short-term advantage — is inherently costly. It means sacrificing expediency, enduring discomfort, and tolerating dissent one has the power to silence. That is why principled actors are rare, and why they are indispensable: without them, political landscapes devolve into competing authoritarianisms, each justifying its abuses by citing the other's excesses, forever. Principled actors provide stability, reduce transactional friction, and uphold the norms of accountability that no rule can enforce on its own. The requirement is that principles be held as terminal values, not instrumental tactics — valued for what they are, not for what they currently win. Centrism as a discipline is what that terminal commitment looks like in office. Its practitioner defends the speech rights of people whose speech he detests, preserves the institutional frictions that currently frustrate his own side, and constrains powers he could use well because his successors might not. None of this is moderation of belief. It is the refusal to let belief, however intense, exempt itself from the constraints that make correction possible. What the Discipline Promises The positive ethos, assembled: pluralism grounded in constraint rather than in relativism. Agency over purity. Coercion treated as a costly instrument, never as a moral reward for being right. Reversibility, feedback, and institutional memory as design criteria. And the standing acknowledgment that no political arrangement resolves all tensions — politics remains an ongoing coordination problem, not a final reckoning, and progress appears as incremental improvement punctuated by necessary rupture where agency is systematically suppressed. Centrism, understood this way, does not promise moral satisfaction. It promises survivability under uncertainty. It treats power as hazardous, certainty as brittle, and agency as the condition under which correction remains possible. In a world shaped by irreversible choices and incomplete knowledge, this posture is not timid; it is exacting. It asks political systems to remain governable even when they are wrong, and it asks political actors to design for that inevitability. That requirement does not inspire chants. It does something harder: it keeps open the space in which correction, pluralism, and future choice remain possible. But a discipline for wielding hazardous power is still a discipline for managing a hazard, and it invites a further question: whether the hazard must be wielded at all — whether politics, in the coercive sense, is a permanent feature of human coordination or an exploit that can be engineered away. That question opens the final part of this volume, beginning with The Conversion of Coercion.

title: The Conversion of Coercion
subtitle: Politics as exploit; civilization as its replacement
volume: Volume 7 — Liberty, Coercion, and Governance
content: There is a line that circulates whenever someone announces they want nothing to do with politics, and it always lands as a mic drop: Saying "I don't do politics" is like saying "I don't do gravity." You can ignore it, but it's not going to ignore you. It's clever. It is also wrong, and wrong in a way worth taking apart slowly, because the error it commits is the single most effective rhetorical defense that political power possesses. The line trades on an equivocation — a linguistic sleight of hand that makes cynicism sound like realism. The trick lies in redefining politics from its proper meaning — the struggle over coercive power — into a catch-all term for any kind of human coordination. Once you equate politics with coordination, the statement becomes tautological: of course you can't avoid politics if every social interaction counts as politics. But that is a rhetorical illusion, not a philosophical truth. Exposing the illusion matters here because this volume has so far been mostly diagnosis. Six parts have examined coercion and its licenses, rights and their forging, speech and its boundaries, law, the egalitarian temptation, and the recurring pathologies of political life — ending with Centrism as a Discipline, the temperament that survives those pathologies: govern cautiously, because society is path-dependent and cascade-prone, and agency is the condition under which correction remains possible. The natural objection to all of it is the one the aphorism compresses: you can criticize politics all you like, but politics is simply what humans do; there is no outside. This final part answers that objection. There is an outside, we have been building it for ten thousand years, and the building of it has a name. It is called civilization. Politics Is Not Coordination Politics, properly defined, is about who gets to use coercion — who can compel others, enforce rules, and wield authority backed by the credible conditional threat of material setback. Coordination, by contrast, is about voluntary alignment — how agents cooperate toward shared or compatible goals. A committee negotiating a technical standard, a market clearing a price, two neighbors agreeing on a fence line: these are coordination. A faction capturing the standards body so that its patents become mandatory, a legislature fixing the price, one neighbor rezoning the other's yard by majority vote: these are politics. The activities can occupy the same room, and that is exactly why the distinction has to be drawn with care rather than dissolved with a quip. Conflating the two erases the crucial moral boundary between voluntary association and imposed hierarchy. It's like saying "all motion is gravity" — poetically appealing, but analytically useless. And the conflation is not an innocent imprecision. By calling all coordination political, the aphorism normalizes coercion. It hides the unique moral danger of politics: that it authorizes some people to rule others. When you accept that everything is politics, you accept domination as inevitable — and worse, as natural. That is how power maintains itself: by convincing the governed that participation is the only moral stance. "You can't avoid politics" becomes code for "you can't avoid being ruled." The move belongs to the same family as the fictions examined in Fictions of the Collective — the national interest, the collective will — verbal constructions whose function is not to describe the world but to make a particular arrangement of power look like a fact of nature. Where those fictions manufacture a collective agent whose will the rulers conveniently channel, this one manufactures a universal medium, politics-as-gravity, inside which the ruled conveniently swim. A subtler version of the move concedes that politics can go wrong but insists the remedy is more and better politics. This frames the issue as good politics versus bad politics , implying that politics itself is neutral — only its practice corrupts. But that misses the structural point: politics, as coercive coordination, incentivizes corruption. Concentrate the authority to compel, and capturing that authority becomes an unusually valuable investment; the pathologies cataloged in Part VI can follow from that incentive, not merely from a shortage of virtuous politicians.
