Enforcement, capture resistance, succession, amendment, insolvency, emergency authority, and protection for agents without purchasing power remain open.

title: The Story-Telling Ape
subtitle: Narrative as cognition's native format
volume: Volume 8 — Culture, Memetics, and Ideology
content: There may have been a man behind King Arthur — a post-Roman warlord in the fog of fifth-century Britain, or perhaps nothing at all but a name attached to other men's deeds. There was almost certainly a man behind Socrates, vouched for by contemporaries who loved him and by contemporaries who did not. There was very probably a man behind Jesus — a Galilean preacher executed under Pilate — though the surviving Christian and later non-Christian sources leave most of the biography contested. Three differently evidenced historical kernels. In every case, what can be defended historically is dwarfed by a cultural structure of incomparable size — the romance of Camelot, the eternal questioner of the dialogues, the incarnate Logos who became the axis of empires. The kernel of a man became the cornerstone of cathedrals. This is not an accident of these three cases. It is what human beings reliably do to their own past, and it points to something about the kind of animal we are. We are the ape that cannot leave a fact alone. Give us a name and a rumor and we will return meaning, drama, and moral weight, whether or not the record supports it. To understand culture — its transmission, its wars, its capture by ideology, the whole arc this volume traces — you have to start with this appetite and take it seriously as engineering, not as a failing. The appetite is not a bug in an otherwise truth-seeking machine. It is the machine. The Substrate Start with the evolutionary hypothesis in its strongest plausible form. We remain primates whose brains evolved under intense pressures from social life. The neural systems supporting executive control and language help us model the physical world and share models with other minds, fast enough to coordinate a band of hunters, settle a dispute, or teach a child what to fear. Narrative is one powerful format that hardware imposes on experience. A story organizes raw events into a shape a listener can hold: agents with intentions, actions with consequences, a beginning that motivates an end. The potential adaptive payoff is enormous, and it runs on three channels at once. Stories carry cooperation — a shared account of who we are and what we owe each other turns a crowd into a group. They codify norms — a parable about the man who betrayed his hosts does the work of a statute without a court to enforce it. And they accelerate learning — a hunter who hears the tale of the flooded ravine need not drown in it himself. These functions make narrative capacity a plausible target or by-product of selection, though they do not reconstruct its exact evolutionary history. An animal that thinks in stories learns from experiences it never had. But humans are not purely biological creatures. Richard Dawkins introduced the meme [^dawkins-meme] to name a culturally transmitted variant tracked by analogy with genes. The analogy is useful when a study can identify variants, carriers, transmission, and differential retention; it does not establish that culture consists of discrete gene-like replicators. Brains, artifacts, institutions, and media let stories be copied and altered under competition for attention and memory. Biological and cultural inheritance then interact: genes help build capacities for social learning, while learned practices reshape the environments in which people develop and reproduce. Neither track alone explains the story-telling ape. [^dawkins-meme]: Richard Dawkins, The Selfish Gene , https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/61535.The Selfish Gene. The Fatal Decoupling Now the surgical turn, because the strength of the adaptive story is exactly what makes its failure mode invisible. Concede everything above and one question remains: what property of a story determines its memetic fitness? What makes one account outcompete another in the arena of retelling? Not truth alone. Transmission can be driven by emotional resonance, moral clarity, social bonding, institutional authority, repetition, and practical success. Accuracy is one fitness factor among several, weak in some environments and decisive in others. A flat true account may lose to a thrilling false one in an attention market; a false map can lose immediately where prediction and material feedback are unforgiving. The channels that made narrative adaptive reward coherence and resonance directly, while rewarding accuracy unevenly through the consequences and correction mechanisms available. This is the dangerous decoupling, and it is not a moralizing complaint about human weakness. Where the operative filters reward resonance more reliably than accuracy, the represented population of stories will tend to move toward resonance. No single “fitness function” need exist: retelling, ranking algorithms, prestige, censorship, and audience choice can impose different filters. Human reason can correct the bias, especially where claims are tested and dissent is protected, but it cannot assume that a story's popularity is evidence of its fit to the world. The map that soothes sometimes beats the map that fits. Hold onto the word pattern here, because it will do heavy lifting for the rest of this volume. A story is one kind: a configuration re-identifiable across tellings and implemented in memories, performances, and records. Its boundaries depend on what the analysis treats as invariant, and its lineage depends on actual transmission rather than resemblance alone. The full model of patterns in cultural selection comes later; for now the point is that stories are not mere decoration laid over cognition. They are a powerful format for organizing and sharing it, and their propagation need not track their accuracy. The Self as a Story The decoupling reaches all the way inward, into the one thing we are most certain we know directly: ourselves. A human self is not transparently discovered by introspection; it is partly maintained through stories under continuous construction — memories, aspirations, values, and grievances woven into a protagonist with continuity across time. This is not ornamental. Narrative is one mechanism by which a bundle of processes represents the person who can make a promise on Monday and keep it on Friday; embodiment, memory, control, relationship, and causal continuity also matter. The architecture underneath this belongs to another volume. The Modeler-Schema Theory distinguishes a role that composes narrative, selects actions, uses language, and reports from a proposed process that generates experience; its secure lesson is that introspective narration is systematically incomplete, while the exact phenomenal division remains a hypothesis (A Candidate Architecture of Consciousness). What matters for culture is the downstream consequence. If the self is partly narrative, then the same forces that select for resonant stories about the tribe also select for resonant stories about me — and a person will defend the flattering self-narrative against contrary evidence with the same tenacity a culture defends its founding myth. The individual and collective cases share selection pressures without thereby constituting one mind. Collective identities — tribal, national, religious — are built from shared stories that bind individuals into a unit by giving them a common protagonist and a common past. What holds a nation together is not only a list of facts. It is also a plot. How Legend Colonizes History Return now to Arthur, Socrates, and Jesus, because they are not three curiosities but an illustrative comparison of decoupling at work on the historical record. History can begin from scattered details, unevenly remembered and recorded, while later tellings accrete story, pattern, and meaning. The useful, resonant version can grow over the thin factual core until the two are difficult to separate. The mechanism has a name worth borrowing from the theory of argument: the motte-and-bailey . The motte is the modest, defensible claim — the dry fact a historian can actually support. The bailey is the expansive structure of meaning, myth, and ideology built on top of it. When the legend is challenged, its defenders retreat to the motte: of course we only claim a real preacher lived and died. When it is unchallenged, they inhabit the bailey: the cosmic savior, the incarnate Logos, the axis of salvation. The two claims share a name and almost nothing else, and the ambiguity between them is not sloppiness — it is the structure that lets the large claim borrow the small claim's credibility. Arrange the three cases by the strength of the motte and the proposed mechanism stands out cleanly. Arthur's motte is feeble — perhaps a warlord, perhaps nothing — yet his bailey is a complete romance of national identity: Camelot, Guinevere, Excalibur, Avalon, none of it from archaeology and all of it from Geoffrey of Monmouth, Chrétien de Troyes, and Malory. Socrates' motte is strong; he certainly lived, attested by friends and enemies alike. Yet what survives is not the man but the Platonic Socrates, the Xenophontic Socrates, the comic Socrates of Aristophanes — each a mask, each a projection of its author's agenda, the historical man buried beneath layers of philosophy. Jesus is the extreme case: a secure motte, a Jewish preacher executed under Pilate, and a bailey that is nothing less than cosmic — miracle-worker, Messiah, Son of God, Logos incarnate, assembled within decades from apocalyptic vision, messianic prophecy, and Hellenistic theology grafted onto the faint outline of a Galilean rabbi. Where Arthur gained chivalry and Socrates gained philosophy, Jesus gained the universe. No other figure here shows so vast a gap between what can be defended historically and what has been believed culturally. The gradient illustrates how weakly the size of a bailey can be coupled to the strength of its motte. A legend can grow because it is useful — because it gives a people a patron saint of reason, a national myth, an axis of salvation — even when the accretion outruns the evidence. History does not remain history. It can be colonized by legend, and legend can thrive because it is needed rather than because each of its claims is true. I am describing a mechanism here, not passing a verdict. That the Jesus legend outgrew its historical core by the widest margin of the three is evidence about memetic fitness, and it implies nothing, by itself, about whether the tradition built on that core is good or bad for the people who live inside it. Those are different questions, and running them together is a mistake this volume takes pains to avoid. A legend can be almost entirely accreted and still stabilize a civilization, cultivate virtue, and preserve wisdom across centuries — and what legend-colonization looks like from the inside of a functioning tradition, where the exemplar at the center does real normative work regardless of the historical record, is a matter I take up directly further on. The descriptive hypothesis is that legend can overgrow fact where resonance is rewarded more reliably than accuracy. The evaluative claim — whether a given overgrowth serves the people who carry it — needs a separate test, and it gets one. The Arc From Here None of this is model-mediated only in the loose sense. All empirical knowledge is already a map rather than the territory; what the story-telling ape adds is a second layer of selection pressure, in which fit to the mind that carries a story can compete with fit to the world. Culture is that second layer, running at scale, and this volume is a natural history of it. The path runs in five stages. First, patterns themselves — how an analysis identifies cultural variants and the mechanisms that maintain or transmit them. Then their ecology — how people, artifacts, incentives, and institutions create feedback loops that can be symbiotic or parasitic. Then the weapons — rhetorical practices people use to protect claims and disable criticism, of which the motte-and-bailey is only the first. Then capture — how enforcement and selection pressures can reorganize an institution around preserving a pattern or faction. And finally the cases — gender, grievance, antisemitism, and other live controversies — where the apparatus is tested against evidence and alternatives. The recurring danger is not a cultural animal secretly choosing through us. It is a human system repeatedly rewarding the story that resonates over the account that fits.

title: Schemas and Groups
subtitle: A toy model of cultural membership
volume: Volume 8 — Culture, Memetics, and Ideology
content: Listen to any argument about culture and you will hear one word doing two jobs. "Christian culture shaped Europe" — is that a claim about a body of ideas or about a population of people? "Immigrants should adopt our culture" — adopt what, exactly: a set of beliefs, or membership in a group? "Western culture is in decline" — are the ideas losing coherence, or are the people who hold them losing numbers? The disputants slide between the two readings, often within a single sentence, and the slide is not harmless. It lets someone defend a set of ideas by pointing to the virtues of a population, or condemn a population by pointing to the vices of a set of ideas. Most of what passes for disagreement about culture is two people equivocating in opposite directions. The fix is to split the word. "Culture" denotes two distinct objects, and once they are named separately, a surprising amount of structure falls out for free. Two Objects, One Word A Cultural Schema is an analyst-specified collection of beliefs, values, preferences, practices, or norms used to model a culture. It is not what a culture literally believes: cultures do not necessarily form agents, their contents are contested, and people instantiate them partially and unevenly. For a deliberately crisp toy model, represent a schema as a set: where each is a modeled belief or value. (What a belief is — not a sentence stored in a head but a feature of a model of an agent — is settled in What Beliefs Are. Here the set notation suppresses degrees of commitment, contradictions, practices, interpretation, and change. Its deductions are conditional on that idealization.) A schema-induced group is the set of agents who satisfy a stated membership rule for that schema. Under the toy model's all-or-nothing rule: where is the modeled belief system of agent . Empirical applications will usually need a threshold, graded membership, observed practice, self-identification, or some combination. A historically identified community is not interchangeable with whichever set this formula produces. Schemas are models; groups are collections of people. A recorded schema can have no current instances, and a historically continuous group can outlive large revisions of its schema. Without records or implementations, however, an alleged extinct schema is a reconstruction rather than a free-standing object. Keeping schema, population, and institution apart is the whole trick. The function is one possible bridge between the first two, not their identity. A Toy Culture The machinery is easiest to see at miniature scale. Take three agents: - with beliefs - with beliefs - with beliefs Define two schemas: and . Then — the agents whose belief systems contain both and — while : everyone, since everyone holds . Notice what just happened. The larger schema, , picked out the smaller group. Adding a belief to a schema adds a requirement for membership, and every added requirement can only shrink the pool of agents who satisfy all of them. Demanding schemas have exclusive groups; permissive schemas have inclusive ones. In general, if — if one schema is contained in another — then: Under these definitions, the subset relation inverts on its way from schema-space to induced group-space. This is a useful property of the model, not an empirical law about identity. We say Catholicism is “part of” Christianity, meaning Catholics are among Christians — a group-space statement. In the toy schema-space, the Catholic schema contains the stipulated Christian core and adds to it. Whenever culture-talk feels paradoxical, check whether a schema claim, population claim, institutional claim, or self-identification is being read as another. Schemas Within Schemas Analysts often arrange schemas into hierarchies, where a stipulated core is shared by more demanding variants. In the toy model, intersections and unions generate a lattice. Whether its nodes correspond to meaningful cultural identities is an empirical and interpretive question, not something set algebra decides. Take the obvious case. Let the Catholic and Protestant schemas be: - - where and are the shared core — the divinity of Christ, the authority of scripture — while and are the distinctives: papal authority on one side, sola fide on the other. The two schemas share , and that intersection is itself a schema — the Christian schema: In this representation, the parent is the features the analyst has encoded as common to its children. Because it is the smaller set, the inversion delivers a hierarchy in both modeled spaces. In schema-space: Therefore, in group-space: Picture the group-space version as nested circles: one large circle, , containing everyone who holds the shared core ; inside it, two smaller regions — , those who also hold , and , those who also hold — overlapping only in the odd agent who holds both distinctives at once. Every Catholic is a Christian; not every Christian is a Catholic; and the reason is nothing deeper than set inclusion running through the function . The construction iterates in both directions. Intersections and unions exist mathematically for every pair of encoded schemas, but a nonempty intersection need not constitute a socially recognized parent, and a union need not describe a possible identity. “Abrahamic,” “Christian,” and “world culture” require historical and semantic arguments in addition to shared entries in a model. Within its limits, the lattice shows a genuine tradeoff: adding mandatory criteria cannot enlarge the population that satisfies all of them. What the Lattice Buys A formalism is worth its notation only if it clarifies things that were murky without it. This one pays for itself three times over. Cultural transmission can be recorded as movement between modeled memberships. Some learners acquire a broad vocabulary before denominational distinctives; others acquire a local practice first and only later learn an abstract parent identity. The lattice organizes observations but does not predict the direction of learning without a transmission mechanism. Cultural divergence can be represented as a split in schema-space when a difference becomes criterial for membership. The Reformation can be schematized that way, but historical explanation still needs institutions, interests, media, doctrine, violence, and contingency that the notation omits. Cultural convergence can be represented by removing or relaxing membership criteria, although shared action and institutional reconciliation need not follow from formal overlap. The hierarchy also suggests a conflict heuristic: look for independently verified shared commitments rather than negotiating only at the point of difference. The formal intersection merely proposes candidates. It does not prove that every member endorses them, that the terms mean the same thing on both sides, or that common belief can settle a conflict driven by power or material interests. “We are all children of Abraham” may open an interfaith conversation; whether it lands is evidence, not algebra. The Special Case I have been describing culture as if it sits still — sets frozen in place, agents whose belief systems hold long enough to be measured against a schema. That is a deliberate idealization, and this chapter comes first in the theory because of it: a lattice of sets is easy to hold in the mind, and the statics are worth mastering before the dynamics. But the reader should know that this is the still photograph, not the film. The moving picture is the subject of Patterns as Players. A cultural schema is one analyst-specified pattern type, and is one modeled population of its current instances. The synchronic slice says who meets the criteria now and how those criteria nest. A dynamic account must separately specify copying, teaching, enforcement, deliberate revision, differential retention, and environmental change. Neither the schema nor the population automatically becomes an agent or player. That reframing has consequences the static model cannot express. Nothing in set notation distinguishes independently supported beliefs from defenses that insulate other beliefs or punish exit. Both are just sets of 's. In practice they behave differently because people and institutions enact different feedback mechanisms. The Egregoric Singularity offers a vivid model of those distributed loops without turning a schema into a literal organism or mind. So take the formalism for what it is: a toy case where culture holds still long enough to be diagrammed. Splitting schema, population, and institution blocks important equivocations; the inverse relation shows why adding mandatory criteria narrows an induced group; the lattice can propose shared commitments for investigation. Its cleanliness comes from what it omits, and every empirical use must put the omitted heterogeneity, history, and agency back in.

title: Patterns as Players
subtitle: A model of cultural persistence
volume: Volume 8 — Culture, Memetics, and Ideology
content: Somewhere in every large organization there is a form that requires three signatures. Nobody knows why three. The rule was instituted decades ago, after a scandal nobody can now describe, by a committee whose members have all retired or died. The scandal is forgotten, the committee dissolved, the original threat long extinct — and the form endures, collecting its three signatures, consuming its small daily tax of attention, training each new cohort of employees to treat it as how things are done. The people churn. The procedure persists. Scale that observation up and it becomes strange. A religion maintains its doctrines through the collapse of the empires that carried it. An outrage cycle runs its identical choreography — the offending remark, the pile-on, the apology, the meta-commentary about the pile-on — on Usenet in 1994, on web forums in 2005, on Twitter in 2020, executed each time by people who have never heard of the previous performances. A corporation's incentive structure survives three complete turnovers of its leadership, quietly converting each fresh, reform-minded executive into a defender of the very dynamics they arrived to change. A movement drifts, decade by decade, away from its founding mission, and no member ever decides that it should. The standard way to explain these things is to point at people. Find the bureaucrat who loves red tape, the cynical executive, the bad-faith activist. And the standard explanation keeps failing, because when you go looking for the culprits you mostly find ordinary people behaving reasonably inside their local circumstances. Everyone is doing something explicable; the system is doing something no one chose. The failure is not in the people. It is in the unit of analysis. The Wrong Unit of Analysis Every visible system — political, scientific, cultural, technological — appears to be driven by individuals making choices. Individuals do make the choices and remain responsible for them. But they are not always the most useful units for explaining cultural persistence. Patterns can be. When a scientist publishes for prestige, a politician signals loyalty, a corporation chases quarterly metrics, or a movement drifts from its mission, a pattern-level model can reveal what an inventory of intentions misses: a stable configuration of behavior and incentives is being reproduced. Patterns do not learn, want, choose, or bear responsibility. People and organizations do those things. The selection claim is narrower: variants that induce people to copy, reward, or enforce them become more common, while variants that do not tend to disappear. “Publish striking novel results,” for example, can persist because career incentives repeatedly reward the people who enact it. Pattern language compresses that causal loop; it does not add another mind to the system. This is the claim that anchors everything else in this volume, so I should say precisely what it quantifies over. What a Pattern Is A pattern is a coherent informational or physical configuration that can be re-identified at a stated grain and that is maintained, copied, or causally influential across the comparison being made. Every clause is load-bearing. Informational or physical : the same procedure may be implemented in a binder, a database, and the habits of a night shift, but it exists only through particular carriers and performances. Configuration : a pattern is an arrangement of parts, not a free-floating substance. At a stated grain : whether two performances count as instances of one pattern depends on the features and tolerable transformations chosen for the analysis. Maintained, copied, or causally influential : resemblance alone does not establish a lineage. A claim about descent also needs a transmission path or other causal continuity. Patterns can be behavioral (habits, routines), cognitive (beliefs, frames), institutional (procedures, norms), cultural (rituals, symbols), technological (architectures, protocols), or economic (pricing heuristics, growth dynamics). A morning routine is a pattern; so is the common law. In each case the analyst owes an identity criterion: which differences are variants of the pattern, which mark a successor, and which end the comparison. Pattern types are equivalence classes under those criteria; pattern tokens are their particular implementations. The type is useful abstraction, not an additional object acting behind its tokens. The definition is deliberately broad, but it does not make every pattern a unit of selection. The model of the previous chapter is a special case in which an analyst specifies a belief-set and a threshold for instantiation. The three-signature form is not a belief; it is a pattern maintained through documents, training, enforcement, and compliant action. Whether either case supports a selection explanation is a further question. Why Patterns Win or Lose A cultural selection account must identify variants, a transmission or retention mechanism, differential outcomes, an environment, and a time horizon. Internal coherence and incentive fit often matter, but so do copying fidelity, teaching and media channels, institutional power, resource constraints, network structure, deliberate revision, and chance. Where those mechanisms are absent, “selection” is a suggestive analogy rather than an explanation. Selection does not by itself select for goodness, truth, or virtue. Under a specified environment and horizon, variants that people copy, reward, enforce, or preserve more effectively gain relative representation. Accuracy can matter greatly where error has visible costs and correction works; resonance, loyalty, coercion, or luck can dominate elsewhere. “Fitness” names that local propagation or persistence outcome. It is not an intrinsic property of an idea, an objective represented by the pattern, or a verdict on its worth. This is why intention alone often explains too little. A flattering false idea can outcompete a burdensome true one in an environment that rewards flattery; a truth can dominate where prediction, audit, or material consequence rewards accuracy. To explain which variant gained ground, ask what people valued, what institutions enforced, what channels transmitted, what alternatives were available, and what the relevant filters rewarded. Patterns Outlive Their Hosts People die. Institutions churn. Regimes collapse. Yet patterns continue. The bureaucracy preserves its procedures long after anyone remembers why they exist. The religion maintains doctrines through centuries of upheaval. The outrage cycle persists across platforms and generations. Corporate incentive structures survive entire leadership turnovers. Cultural norms endure migrations, wars, and technological shocks. In each case the informational structure has decoupled its lifespan from the lifespans of its hosts, because what sustains it is not any particular person's commitment but the incentive gradient that keeps recruiting new people into the roles the pattern defines. This qualifies the intuitive picture of agency: we operate through inherited patterns, and inherited patterns constrain what we notice and choose. The language you argue in, the career script you are following, the moral reflexes you deploy without deliberation, the institutional procedures you enact at work — you executed few of their design decisions. The patterns predate you; they were shaped by selection pressures you never witnessed; they may recruit your successors after you are gone. Much choosing begins from inherited scripts. Until you see this, you will keep trying to fix systems only by replacing their people, and you will keep being amazed that the replacements encounter the same incentives. The Pattern Economy Patterns do not persist in isolation. They can be modeled within a competitive ecology — a pattern economy — where implementations interact, change, conflict, and propagate. Its “currencies” are metaphors for measurable dimensions: stability, copying rate, adaptability, coherence, and reach. The exchange rates vary by mechanism and horizon. Some patterns are self-reinforcing: each execution strengthens the conditions for the next, the way a credential requirement entrenches itself by populating hiring committees with the credentialed. Others decay unless actively maintained, the way a norm of rigorous peer review survives only as long as someone pays its costs. A high-propagation pattern may be embedded in budgets, procedures, and careers; that result is produced by decisions, enforcement, and path dependence, not by the pattern commandeering an institution as an agent would. This ecology need not track any one person's preference. Its aggregate result reflects what people and institutions repeatedly reward, copy, or enforce; “performance” here means persistence, not virtue. Incentives as Pattern Filters What helps set the exchange rates in the pattern economy? Incentives. I have argued elsewhere that formal rules and effective incentives can diverge. Here the same machinery appears one level up: incentives shape what individuals do and thereby filter which patterns are retained. They are one family of filters, alongside deliberate judgment, transmission constraints, law, material limits, and stochastic drift. Scientific prestige rewards novelty rather than accuracy, so novelty-generating patterns dominate scientific discourse, and replication — true, dull, essential — is left to volunteers. Media ecosystems reward attention, so attention-maximizing patterns drive information flows, and the measured take loses to the incendiary one on every metric a platform can see. Politics rewards loyalty, so loyalty-signaling patterns outperform competence, and the skill of visibly belonging crowds out the skill of governing. Markets reward growth, so growth-seeking patterns displace sustainable ones wherever the horizon of accountability is shorter than the horizon of consequence. Prestige filters for novelty; media filter for attention; politics filters for loyalty; markets filter for growth. In each arena the institution's stated values — truth, information, service, prosperity — describe what the filter is supposed to pass. What it passes is whatever matches its gradient. Patterns drift toward what incentives reinforce, not toward what institutions claim to value. Write that sentence over the door of every reform movement, because it is the epitaph of most of them: reformers replace the people and preserve the filter, and the filter regrows the pattern. Drift, Lock, Collapse Patterns mutate as they replicate — every retelling, every reimplementation, every new hire's imperfect imitation introduces variation, and the incentive environment selects among the variants. Three characteristic pathologies fall out of this dynamic, and they recur so often throughout this volume that they need fixed names. Pattern drift occurs when accumulated changes gradually shift a pattern away from its original purpose. No single mutation is large enough to trigger resistance; the sum is transformation. This is the general form of mission drift: the charity that becomes a fundraising apparatus, the regulator that becomes an industry concierge, the university that becomes a credential vendor. Each step was locally reasonable. The direction was set by the incentive gradient, not by anyone's intention. Pattern lock occurs when a pattern reaches a self-reinforcing equilibrium that persists even when harmful — when the pattern has arranged its environment so that every escape path costs more than staying. This is the general form of bureaucratic stagnation, and it is also the general form of the echo chamber: a community whose filtering practices reinforce the beliefs that justify the filtering practices has locked, and a later chapter traces what that lock does to a culture's capacity for error correction. The mark of lock is that the pattern's dysfunction becomes an argument for the pattern — every failure of the locked system is read, from inside, as proof that more of the system is needed. Pattern collapse occurs when coherence fails: replication becomes too noisy, competing patterns overwhelm it, or the costs of maintaining coherence exceed what the environment pays for it. The pattern stops being one thing, and then it stops being a thing at all. This is the general form of ideological implosion — the belief system that fragments into warring interpretations, each too small to sustain the institutions the whole once commanded. Drift explains mission drift. Lock explains stagnation. Collapse explains implosion. The dynamics are analogous to natural selection — variation, inheritance, differential persistence — but the analogy has limits. Cultural variants are deliberately revised, transmitted unevenly, and filtered by reflective agents; “fitness” is therefore a local description of persistence under specified conditions, not a biological quantity imported whole. A Note on Attractors One more piece of vocabulary needs fixing here, because this volume will use the word “attractor” at three different scales. In a specified dynamical model, an attractor is a state or region toward which nearby trajectories tend and within which they remain. That claim requires a state space, dynamics, and basin. Elsewhere in this volume, attractor is an analogy for a recurrent or stabilizing influence; it must not borrow mathematical necessity from the technical term. At the scale of individual behavior, an exemplar can orient imitation, which is the next chapter's subject. At the scale of belief systems, an ideology can make nearby revisions costly — the black-hole metaphor of the geometry of culture. At the scale of civilizations, some arrangements recur as coordination points — the subject of the volume's oldest case. These cases may share feedback structures, but they do not thereby share one equation. Choosing the Patterns You Serve There is a deeper level still — the persistence of patterns not across institutions or generations but across the fundamental constraints of physical reality — and it belongs to the metagame sequence developed in earlier volumes rather than here. What belongs here is the human consequence. Most action is patterned. You instantiate strategies, norms, behaviors, and identities that predate you and will outlast you; on any given day, very little of what you do was designed by you. This sounds like a counsel of despair, and it is the opposite. You cannot opt out of running patterns — an agent stripped of every inherited pattern is not free, merely incompetent, like a speaker with no language. Reflective agency adds something no pattern can do for itself: evaluating which patterns you propagate, which you resist, which you nurture, and which you extinguish. That capacity is only as good as the test it applies, and "does this pattern feel right?" is no test at all — feeling right is precisely what successful patterns install in their hosts. The filter has to be built deliberately, and building it is the next chapter's work: the Axionic Criterion, a standard for which patterns deserve propagation that does not simply reward the patterns best at seeming to deserve it. Understanding patterns reveals architecture beneath behavior, institutions, and culture — why systems drift while personnel change, why intentions can lose to incentives, and why similar dramas restage themselves with fresh casts. Pattern-level explanation and human agency are complements: the first identifies recurring causal organization; the second locates interpretation, choice, intervention, and responsibility.

title: Exemplars and the Axionic Criterion
subtitle: How patterns travel, and which deserve to
volume: Volume 8 — Culture, Memetics, and Ideology
content: A child does not learn to stand by consulting a rule. She watches, sways, falls, adjusts, and tries again, guided by the moving example of another body already balanced. No proposition passes between them. No one could state the proposition if asked. What passes is a pattern — a configuration of posture and correction that the child's nervous system absorbs, rehearses, and eventually owns. That process never retires. We like to imagine that adult competence graduates from imitation to calculation, that somewhere in adolescence we trade watching for reasoning. We do not. Adult agency continues to run on absorbed patterns rather than explicit computation. The surgeon's hands, the negotiator's timing, the parent's judgment about when to intervene and when to let a child struggle — none of these were learned from manuals, and none could be fully written down. They were caught, not taught. Skills, norms, and values propagate through lived examples that can be perceived, compressed, and recomposed, which means cultural inheritance proceeds through embodied behavior at least as much as through instruction. This is one mechanism through which developed agency acquires competence: internalizing action-patterns and deploying them flexibly under changing conditions. It is not a new definition of agency; the embedded model–evaluation–control loop remains the canonical core. Patterns as Players made the case that analyst-specified pattern types are useful units for tracking cultural selection, while people remain the choosing and responsible agents through whom transmission occurs. This chapter is about that transmission channel — how patterns move from body to body — and about the normative question the volume has been building toward: of all the patterns competing to move through us, which ones deserve to? Exemplars as Behavioral Attractors Open-ended environments demand judgment under variation. No rulebook anticipates every situation; the situations that matter most are precisely the ones the rulebook missed. What stabilizes action under novelty is not a longer rulebook but a reference pattern — a worked example of how someone handles the class of problem well. An exemplar is an agent whose behavior functions as an attractor in behavioral space. Where Patterns as Players distinguished the three scales of attraction this volume tracks, this is the smallest and most intimate: not a Schelling point that coordinates strangers, not a black hole that captures a worldview, but a lived pattern that orients individual action. Exemplars shape what an agent notices, what she expects, what possibilities appear open to her. Around a genuine exemplar, the space of things one might do acquires a gradient. An apprentice watches a master carpenter cut a joint. The lesson does not arrive as a proposition. It arrives as posture, timing, pressure, restraint. The pattern embeds itself and later re-emerges through the apprentice's hands — not as a memory of the master, but as a way of being a carpenter. This is the ordinary miracle on which every craft, every profession, and every moral tradition depends. An exemplar's influence scales with three properties of the associated pattern. Coherence : the pattern hangs together — its parts reinforce rather than contradict one another, so that adopting one piece pulls the others along. Generality : it transfers — the carpenter's restraint is legible to the surgeon, the master's patience to the parent. Compressibility : it can be carried in a small package — a story, a maxim, a remembered gesture — and unpacked at the point of need. A pattern strong on all three axes can leap across centuries and cultures on the strength of a parable. A pattern weak on all three dies with its first host. And exemplars persist through reinterpretation, not despite it. Agents selectively adopt, modify, and recombine aspects of a reference pattern as their conditions change. Over time this is evolutionary selection operating on action-patterns: variation in each new instantiation, selection by what continues to work, retention in the bodies and stories of those who carry it forward. Lineages and the River Cultural continuity is the persistence of shared reference patterns across generations. Lineages form around exemplars whose patterns remain legible enough to perceive, teachable enough to transmit, and adaptable enough to survive contact with new circumstances. Religious figures are history's highest-bandwidth exemplars. Their narratives encode dense bundles of behavior, motivation, and constraint — not a list of rules but a personality one can consult, a compressed answer to the question what would he do? These bundles propagate through repetition, reinterpretation, and partial instantiation across enormous populations and spans of time. No other transmission technology in the historical record comes close. The Story-Telling Ape described what this looks like from the outside: legend colonizes fact, the historical kernel disappears under the accumulating bailey of story, and the Jesus of history becomes unrecoverable beneath the Jesus of faith. That account is true, and it is the descriptive half of the picture. But it invites a mistaken inference — that because the legend outran the man, the pattern is therefore fraudulent, a mere artifact of ravenous imagination. The functional question is separate from the historical one. Whether the kernel survives excavation tells us nothing about whether the pattern works: whether the bundle of behaviors the tradition transmits — the forgiveness under provocation, the dignity extended downward, the refusal to return violence — supports the agency of those who instantiate it. Mythogenesis explains how the pattern got its vehicle. It does not evaluate the cargo. That evaluation needs a different instrument, and this chapter builds it. A pattern that survives centuries does so the way a river survives: by flowing, branching, eroding obstacles, and reshaping itself while retaining a recognizable course. The Danube is not the same water, the same banks, or even quite the same route it was a thousand years ago, yet it is unmistakably the same river. So with a living tradition. Persistence of this kind is not inertia. It records successful transmission under changing conditions, but not one verdict on why: agents may find a pattern useful or worth its cost, while family inheritance, institutional support, coercion, path dependence, and chance also keep traditions flowing. Reading "Lord" as Pattern Centrality Within a lineage, compressed phrases do diagnostic work. When a believer says "Jesus is Lord," a metaphysical reading takes this as a claim about the governance of the cosmos, and the argument immediately becomes one about evidence for supernatural facts — an argument that has been stuck for centuries because the two sides are not discussing the same kind of proposition. Read functionally, the phrase is a diagnostic of pattern centrality. "Lord" designates salience and gravitational pull within a shared pattern space. The phrase marks a convergence point: it announces that this behavioral pattern serves as the common reference against which action gets evaluated within this lineage — the exemplar of exemplars, the pattern to consult when patterns conflict. That centrality arose through adoption, repetition, reinterpretation, institutions, and inheritance across two thousand years of agents. Its continuation demonstrates durable transmission, not that every carrier found the pattern agency-supporting or freely chose it. Whether it now supports agency is a separate question for the Criterion this chapter is about. This reading is neither endorsement nor debunking. It does not require the metaphysics, and it does not require the sneer. It takes the phrase seriously as a report about the structure of a cultural pattern space — which is, I think, more respect than either the apologist or the village atheist typically manages. Coordination Through Attraction Notice what exemplars do not do as exemplars . They do not command or enforce; institutions built around them may. Exemplars constrain behavior through attraction: agents orient toward patterns that appear to support stable coordination, reduce destructive conflict, and preserve their agency across the situations they actually face. Where participation remains interpretive and revisable, nobody instantiates the carpenter or the Christ by rote; each agent can take what fits, adapt what almost fits, and drop what does not. Attraction and usefulness can sustain a pattern, but so can authority, dependency, and inherited default. This yields something remarkable: coordination without an enforcer. When many agents orbit overlapping reference patterns, their expectations about one another align — not perfectly, but enough. The handshake, the queue, the honest weight, the kept promise: these run on shared patterns, not on surveillance. Enforcement exists, but as a backstop for the margins, not as the engine. A society that had to police every norm it depends on would spend everything on police. The rhyme with the political argument of Volume 7 is not accidental — the conversion of coercion makes the same case at the level of institutions that this chapter makes at the level of culture: orders that run on attraction are cheaper, more adaptive, and more durable than orders that run on force. Plurality of exemplars is a further, underrated asset. Different domains sustain different reference patterns — the scientist's exemplars are not the soldier's, the mother's are not the merchant's — with partial overlap providing resilience under environmental change. When one lineage degrades or meets conditions it cannot handle, agents can shift weight to another without the whole coordination fabric tearing. A culture that enforces a single exemplar everywhere has built a pattern monoculture, and monocultures fail the way monocultures always fail: all at once, to the first pathogen adapted to them. What that looks like in practice — communities sealed around one pattern, treating every alternative as contamination — is the subject of Gated Realities. Distributed Instantiation Where does a cultural pattern live? Not in any text, though texts carry compressed versions of it. Not in any institution, though institutions scaffold it. It lives in its instantiations: collective participation takes the form of distributed instantiation of a pattern across agents, each realizing it under local constraints, each contributing marginally to its evolution. This process need not have a headquarters. There is no committee that maintains carpentry, and no single office owns every instantiation of the Sermon on the Mount. Pattern survival depends on continued retention or replication under selective pressure. As environments shift, instantiations diverge where local conditions differ, converge where a variant propagates better under the operative filters, and attenuate where transmission fails. The same dynamic can govern cultural norms, ethical frameworks, and institutional practices — anything transmitted by example, inheritance, enforcement, or sustained use. Distributed instantiation explains both the resilience and the drift of traditions. Resilience, because a pattern spread across a million bodies cannot be killed by destroying any one of them, or any thousand. Drift, because a million local reinterpretations under a million local constraints will carry the pattern somewhere its founders would not recognize. The river again: no single obstacle stops it, and no stretch of it holds still. The Axionic Criterion Everything so far has been descriptive: how patterns transmit, why some persist. The question the whole volume needs answered is normative: which patterns deserve to propagate? Selection alone cannot answer it — Patterns as Players established that the environment rewards performance, not virtue, and history is full of patterns that spread magnificently while hollowing out everyone who carried them. Here is the test. For a pattern to merit propagation through a population of agents, it must demonstrate agency preservation under ongoing instantiation. Concretely, three questions: 1. Does the pattern support coherent choice under constraint? Agents who instantiate it should become more capable of judgment in hard situations, not less — the pattern should function like the carpenter's absorbed skill, extending what its carriers can do. 2. Does it reduce reliance on coercive stabilization? A pattern that can only persist by punishing defectors, silencing critics, or walling off alternatives is confessing that it cannot hold agents by attraction. The police budget of a pattern is a measure of its failure. 3. Does it scale across agents without collapsing autonomy? Some patterns work beautifully at small scale and become machines for obedience at large scale. The test is whether the millionth instantiation is still a choosing agent or has become a component. Call this the Axionic Criterion. It is the volume's instrument, and the chapters that follow will apply it repeatedly — to ideologies, to institutions, to the weaponized discourse patterns of Part III and the capture systems of Part IV. Two clarifications about its standing. First, the Criterion is not a smuggled objective value. Volume 5 argued that value has no agent-independent existence — Phosphorism locates all valuing in valuers — and the Criterion respects that: it does not rank patterns against a cosmic good. Agency is not one value among others; it is the precondition of anything being valued at all. But that is a descriptive fact, and a descriptive fact compels no one's rankings by itself. What the Criterion adds is a choice: this book adopts reciprocal agency preservation as an explicit commitment, and then asks whether a pattern preserves the very capacity that makes valuing possible. A pattern that consumes the agency of its hosts dissolves the ground on which those hosts could call anything good — self-undermining in the same way, and for the same reason, as the ethical systems the viability criterion rules out in Volume 5, rather than wrong by cosmic decree. Second, the Criterion is not administered by a tribunal. The evaluation occurs locally and continuously, in the lives of instantiating agents. Every time someone finds that a tradition helps them choose well under pressure, the pattern passes a trial for that agent under those conditions; every time someone notices that their framework survives in them only through fear of leaving it, the pattern fails one. Passing can support voluntary propagation, and failure can motivate disengagement, reinterpretation, or abandonment, but neither outcome mechanically determines cultural survival. When The Geometry of Culture maps the curved landscape of cultural evolution and confronts the relativism built into it — no neutral vantage, no fixed fitness function — agency preservation will emerge as the leading candidate for a cross-cultural standard: a measure that stays legible across frames because every frame needs agents to hold it, and one this book chooses to privilege rather than reads off the terrain. Selection will not enforce it for us — coercion and lock-in can keep agency-consuming patterns alive — which is why the standard has to be applied, not awaited. The Criterion is that standard made operational: three questions any agent, or any accountable institution, can ask about a pattern reaching for their hands. Civilization is not run from anywhere. It is a fabric of shared action-patterns instantiated by billions of embedded agents, coordinated by attraction to exemplars whose influence rests on coherence, compressibility, and sustained performance. The patterns worth keeping are the ones that carry agency forward — like a river shaping its course, like a craft refined through generations of hands.

title: The Egregoric Singularity
subtitle: The merger already happened
volume: Volume 8 — Culture, Memetics, and Ideology
content: Everyone is waiting for the Singularity. The scenario is familiar to the point of liturgy: some future moment when artificial intelligence outpaces human cognition and history bends around an event we cannot predict. This chapter offers a deliberately provocative comparison. Long before silicon, cumulative culture created distributed systems that outlived individuals and transformed the conditions of human life. Calling that transition an egregoric singularity is a model and metaphor, not a claim that a new biological species or conscious superorganism appeared. Ben Hunt pictures our lives as rooms in grand narrative hotels — Hollywood, Wall Street, Washington, Harvard — institutions that construct worlds we willingly inhabit. His insight is that these institutions are not neutral settings but shape belief, identity, and behavior; he gestures at “ideas with goals.” I go further, but only at the level of modeling. Hunt's “semantic institutions” can be treated as egregores : collective patterns with agency-like regularities, implemented by people, records, incentives, and organizations. When Culture Joined Genes Cumulative culture made inherited language, ritual, law, and story causally important alongside genes. People sometimes sacrifice food, reproduction, or life for doctrines and groups. Such conduct still admits biological, psychological, strategic, and historical explanation; culture does not replace genes as a sovereign controller. The narrower point is that learned symbols and institutions reorganize incentives and identities strongly enough that genetic advantage alone cannot predict individual action. Writing, religion, law, and markets each changed the trajectory of the species, and none is simply a tool we picked up. They are inherited systems that reorganized the choices available to their users. Writing did not just record human thought; it restructured it, allowing arguments to extend beyond the limits of oral memory. Law did not just codify custom; legal orders outlive individual judges and recruit new generations of officers to maintain them. Markets did not just facilitate exchange; they became adaptive systems that no participant designed and no participant can ignore without cost. From the moment these systems existed, human development became simultaneously biological and cultural. "Egregore" is an old occultists' word, and I use it for its vividness, not its metaphysics. Nothing spooky is being claimed. In the vocabulary of this volume, an egregore is simply a pattern — a coherent configuration of information stable enough to exert influence, in the sense of Patterns as Players — that has recruited enough carriers to be defended and reproduced. That last clause motivates the biological analogy. Consider what Hollywood, Wall Street, Washington, and Harvard actually do, as opposed to what their org charts say. They display self-preserving regularities : participants detect threats and mobilize against them, sometimes without central direction. They are reproductive : they generate narratives, rituals, and new cohorts. They are adaptive : they change under competition and selective pressure. These are organism-like properties, but not sufficient evidence of consciousness, intention, or literal life. The model earns its keep only when it explains those distributed regularities more clearly than a list of individual motives would. The Midwife Where does artificial intelligence fit, if not at the origin? AI is an accelerant. Large language models, recommender systems, and algorithmic feeds can reduce the cost and increase the speed, scale, and targeting of cultural production and distribution. Whether a given system actually increases fidelity, reach, polarization, or persuasion is an empirical question requiring platform-specific evidence; “orders of magnitude” should not be inferred from the metaphor. These systems amplify feedback loops that long predate them. But the machines are amplifiers, not origins. The cultural dynamics they accelerate also built cathedrals and stock exchanges. What machine minds themselves are — what they model, whether they understand, what kind of cognition runs in them — is the subject of another volume; see especially Fluency and Its Limits. For this volume's purposes one claim suffices: AI is a powerful instrument of cultural reproduction, and the patterns it amplifies long predate it. The Living Cave If the Singularity is behind us, Plato's Cave needs to be reconceived. In the original allegory, the shadows on the wall are inert illusions, cast by cynical puppeteers, and the philosopher's task is to escape into sunlight. Every element of that picture is now wrong. The shadows behave as if alive. They are not always projected at us by a single manipulator; distributed incentives can arrange many participants into a stable formation. Ideas influence institutions only through people, artifacts, and rules that transmit and enforce them. Whoever you nominate as the cynical manipulator behind the shadow play — the media baron, the party strategist, the algorithm designer — may turn out to be another participant performing an institutionally rewarded role. The shadow play need not be staged deception. It can be the emergent output of a distributed system. The cave is usefully modeled as an organism-like system — an egregore composed of people, myths, symbols, and institutions. Its walls are woven of narrative; its floor is laid with belief; its torches burn with desire and fear. Because every available standpoint uses inherited concepts, there is no culture-free exit. To leave one cavern is to enter another interpretive frame. Even an ideology of liberation supplies its own vocabulary, authorities, and picture of awakening. The recursion is not literally alive, but it is causally real: we are part of the machinery by which frameworks are reproduced. This is where most readers expect despair, and it is exactly where despair is wrong. Agency is scaffolded by inherited language, concepts, and practices, so independence from all cultural influence is neither available nor desirable. The relevant freedom is partial and practical: making influences visible, comparing alternatives, revising commitments, and changing the institutions that reward them. We do not merely serve or starve abstractions; we choose, teach, fund, enforce, and resist particular implementations. Curation requires a criterion, and the living cave supplies one. Some egregores are parasitic: they siphon their hosts' vitality into obedience, consuming interpretation and transmuting meaning into conformity and allegiance. Others are symbiotic: they scaffold coherence — supplying language, structure, and continuity — without erasing the autonomy of their hosts. A parasitic pattern leaves you smaller, more dependent, and more afraid; a symbiotic one leaves you more capable of coherent choice than it found you. The apocalyptic cult that ends with its hosts penniless in a compound is the pure parasite; the scientific tradition — which trains its hosts in methods that can be turned against its own doctrines — is about as symbiotic as an egregore gets. Most of the patterns that matter lie between those poles, and many migrate along the spectrum over their lifetimes, which is why the judgment has to be renewed rather than made once. This distinction is the informal ancestor of the volume's normative test. What I later formalize as the Axionic Criterion in Exemplars and the Axionic Criterion — does the pattern support coherent choice under constraint, reduce reliance on coercive stabilization, and scale across agents without collapsing their autonomy? — is the parasitic/symbiotic distinction made precise. The pathological end of the spectrum gets its own taxonomy in Memetic Pathogens; the terminal stage, in which a pattern persuades its hosts to wall themselves inside it and call the wall safety, is the subject of Gated Realities. Here the point is only the redefinition of agency: authenticity is not the illusion of independence from patterns. It is the conscious choice of which to inhabit, which to empower, and which to resist. The task is not escape but choosing which shadows to feed. The Faith of the Flag All of this can sound abstract until you examine a mature distributed pattern. Take the nation. Some forms of modern nationalism function like secular religions along several dimensions. The comparison can organize evidence about ritual, sacred symbols, founding narratives, taboo, and sacrifice; it does not establish that every nation is a religion or a literal organism. It has sacred symbols and liturgy. Flags, anthems, emblems, and monuments function precisely as religious icons: they evoke reverence, affirm collective identity, and demand ritualized handling. Pledging allegiance, saluting the flag, singing the national hymn, keeping the national holidays — these are secular liturgies, communal acts of reverence whose repetition manufactures loyalty and emotional unity. It has scripture and saints. Every nation tells foundational myths — heroic origins, celebrated founders, defining battles — with the structure and emotional charge of creation stories and hagiography. These narratives legitimize the nation's present identity and policies, and they are installed in each new generation through the educational system, which is to say through catechism. Alongside the saints stand the martyrs: those who die for the nation are honored exactly as religious communities honor those who die for the faith, their sacrifices sanctified through monuments, memorial days, and rites of remembrance that fold personal loss into collective meaning. It has a moral code and a concept of heresy. Nationalism prescribes virtues — patriotism, civic duty, loyalty, courage — and can sort insiders from outsiders. Desecrating symbols or challenging a sacred narrative may provoke stigma, fury, or legal penalty. In the model's compressed vocabulary, “the egregore defends itself”; causally, people and organizations perceive a threat, coordinate a response, and enforce norms through identifiable channels. It has communion, pilgrimage, priesthood, and eschatology. National identity offers belonging and purpose, frequently superseding every other affiliation, uniting strangers into a congregation of millions. Battlefields, shrines, and capitals become sacred sites, pilgrimage destinations where citizens reaffirm their bond to the collective story. Founders and iconic leaders play prophet and high priest, their words quoted as authoritative texts, their persons treated as embodiments of national virtue. And the whole structure points toward a collective destiny — manifest destiny, exceptionalism, the historical mission — a secular redemption that gives individual lives meaning beyond themselves and motivates sacrifice toward a future the sacrificers will never see. Seen this way, nationalism's potency becomes less mysterious. Challenges to national identity can feel like profanation rather than policy disagreement. No single committee had to design the whole package: historical borrowing, deliberate statecraft, imitation, conflict, schooling, and differential retention can accumulate compatible mechanisms. The sacred may migrate as religious participation changes. (I pursue that migration in Secular Sacredness.) Whether a national pattern scaffolds or constrains agency is not settled by the analogy. It must be judged through its actual effects, coercion, alternatives, and institutions. Critical Mass Related feedbacks appear at different scales, but scale changes the relevant unit and mechanism. A national pattern depends on distributed carriers, institutions, and enforcement; a private body of thought can display an analogous accumulation of scaffolding without yet forming a collective lineage. When a body of work grows, it can cross a practical threshold at which shared concepts and references make extension easier. Calling this a phase transition highlights a qualitative change but does not assert a universal critical point or physical law. Early pieces invent framing and terms; later pieces can reuse scaffolding already in place. Three forces drive the acceleration. First, network effects: each new contribution plugs into existing concepts, and every connection strengthens the lattice. Second, reduced cognitive cost: established frameworks carry explanatory power, so the thinker need only choose the right lens rather than grind a new one. Third, compression through language: once coined, a term condenses paragraphs into a word, and intellectual bandwidth expands accordingly. Past the threshold, the body of work itself acts as a constructor — a structure that makes future structures easier to build. The more the system grows, the more it pulls new thought into alignment with itself. What began as scattered sparks becomes a recursive engine of coherence. Read that last sentence again with this chapter's eyes. A lattice that recruits new thought into its own extension, that gets easier to serve the longer you serve it, that compresses its doctrines into transmissible vocabulary — that is an egregore in embryo. The private transition is an analogue and possible precursor, not the same event as the birth of a collective thought-form. The latter requires transmission: other carriers must learn, retain, vary, and extend the pattern. This suggests a heuristic sequence rather than a law. Some intellectual movements pass from discovery, to construction and refinement, to codification and transmission. Others fragment, disappear, or move backward. When a private vocabulary becomes a public tradition, people can teach and extend it without contact with its originator. In egregoric shorthand it has acquired “hosts”; literally, a distributed lineage has formed through identifiable carriers and institutions. The reflexive case is the book you are holding. This book is a lattice past critical mass. The essays it reworks began as high-friction expeditions; somewhere along the way the frameworks interlocked, the coined terms — patterns, egregores, the Axionic Criterion — started doing compression work, and each new piece became easier to write than the last because the constructor was already in place. The acceleration was magnified by dialogue with a dialectical catalyst, artificial as it happens, which lowered the friction of invention and let ideas be tested and sharpened at speed — the mechanism examined in The Dialectic Catalyst. By its own account, then, this book is a young egregore soliciting hosts, and the volume's tests apply to it with full force. I offer it under the symbiotic bargain as I have defined it: judge whether it scaffolds your coherence or demands your obedience, and feed it only if it passes. That is the situation, from civilizational scale down to the page in front of you. Writing, faiths, flags, markets, movements, and this book are inherited cultural systems competing for limited attention and support through human and institutional mechanisms. “Living shadows” is the chapter's governing metaphor. Autonomy lies not in pretending to escape inheritance, but in identifying those mechanisms, testing their effects, and deciding — consciously and accountably — which patterns to carry forward.

title: The Geometry of Culture
subtitle: Curved landscapes and black holes
volume: Volume 8 — Culture, Memetics, and Ideology
content: Ideologies are the black holes of the human thought space. Their pull moves adherents past an event horizon that makes it impossible to consider ideas outside of the ideological frame. — Joscha Bach[^bach-black-hole] [^bach-black-hole]: Joscha Bach (@Plinz), post on X, August 2025, https://x.com/Plinz/status/1953922984634462238. The fitness landscape is one of the most durable pictures in evolutionary theory, and it is almost entirely wrong about culture. In biology it earns its keep: genotypes map to phenotypes, phenotypes to survival and reproduction, and the height of the terrain — fitness — is defined by reproductive consequences, not by anything the organism prefers. That terrain is not frozen; frequency-dependence, coevolution, and niche construction all move it, and what an organism does and prefers can be among the causes that move it. (Drift, by contrast, moves a population across the landscape by shifting allele frequencies; it reshapes the terrain only where those shifts then change fitness.) What preference cannot do is rewrite the yardstick. A species does not make fertility count for less by prizing it less; reproductive success keeps its own books. The mountain can shift as the world and its inhabitants change, but never because the climbers decree a new way of measuring height. Borrow that picture for culture and you smuggle in an assumption that quietly destroys it. Cultures do not climb a fixed landscape. They write the yardstick as they move. A pattern's cultural fitness is still just how far it propagates and how well it persists — that much is the same as anywhere. What differs is that the standards deciding which patterns spread — the values, norms, aesthetics, and status signals a culture rewards — are themselves cultural products, and those are precisely the things cultural evolution keeps changing. When the reward criteria drift, yesterday's high-fitness pattern becomes today's low-fitness one — not because anyone moved, but because the standards reshaped themselves under their feet. A family that once measured its worth by making music together comes to measure it by shared screen time, and the mountain they were standing on changes into a different mountain. Cultural actors are not climbing the terrain. They are the mass that bends it. The Self-Curved Manifold This is the same structural move general relativity made against Newton. There is no external flat grid against which motion is measured. Mass-energy tells spacetime how to curve, and the curvature tells mass-energy how to move; the geometry is endogenous, self-referential, and it produces trajectories — geodesics — that are perfectly straight from the inside while looking like spirals from anywhere else. Culture has exactly this shape. Let me set the correspondence down plainly, because the whole chapter runs on it. Culture is the mass-energy: the accumulated substance of values, norms, and practices. The fitness function is the curvature: what a given cultural configuration counts as "uphill." And cultural evolution is geodesic motion: each culture following the locally straightest path its own values define. There is no global direction called improvement. Every cultural vantage generates its own metric and then measures progress against it, and what reads as maladaptive under one metric reads as optimal under another. Two pictures make the geometry concrete. The first is the deforming landscape : as a culture moves, the peaks and valleys migrate, so that the act of climbing reshapes what counts as high ground — you never get to finish the ascent because the summit relocates while you walk. The second is the cultural spacetime manifold : values act as sources of curvature, and cultural trajectories bend around these value-masses the way light bends around a star. A culture that prizes autonomy warps the manifold one way; a culture that prizes fertility warps it another; each then experiences its own bent path as the obvious, natural, forward direction. Both pictures say the same thing. The map is not merely failing to match the territory. The territory is actively reconfiguring itself in response to where the map-makers stand. Four Consequences Take the geometry seriously and four things follow that a fixed-landscape model cannot even state. The first is cultural drift , in Robin Hanson's sense.[^hanson-drift] Because a culture writes its own fitness criteria and rewrites them faster than selection can punish the bad ones, societies can drift toward values that quietly undermine their own survival — and never register it as failure, because by the culture's current metric nothing has gone wrong. Fertility is the standing example. What once counted as flourishing, a house full of children, gets recoded as a loss of autonomy, and a civilization can walk into demographic contraction feeling, at every step, that it is doing better. This is the seam where Vol 6's account of the prosperity paradox meets the geometry: the fertility collapse there is drift here, a locally rational reweighting of what a good life contains, running faster than any corrective can catch it. [^hanson-drift]: Robin Hanson, “How Fix Cultural Drift?”, Overcoming Bias , https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/how-fix-cultural-drift. The second is accumulated loss , in Lauren Wilford's sense.[^wilford-loss] Each technological wave displaces an embodied practice — piano to radio to television to the endless scroll — and from inside each step the trade looks like a clear gain. Television is easier than making music; scrolling is more available than conversation. No single substitution feels like a wound. But the losses compound down a channel nobody is watching, because the thing being lost is not any one practice but the habit of embodied co-presence itself, and a habit's disappearance is invisible to a metric that never counted it. The geometry explains why the loss is systematically undercounted: the yardstick that would register it is exactly the thing the drift eroded. You cannot miss what you no longer have the concept to name, and the concept was one of the casualties. [^wilford-loss]: Lauren Wilford (@lauren wilford), post on X, September 2025, https://x.com/lauren wilford/status/1967087944520679582. The third is built-in relativism . From the old standard the new practices look decadent; from the new standard the old ones look oppressive or archaic; and both verdicts are correct within their own frame , because the landscape has bent to fit the values doing the judging. There is no neutral vantage from which to rank the frames without importing the values of one of them — no view from nowhere onto cultural worth. This is not a defect I am introducing; it falls straight out of the endogenous geometry. It is also not a place to stop, because stopping there would be surrender. Vol 2 has already made the general case: the absence of a neutral vantage does not license relativism — it demands better standards, not the abandonment of standards. Here we meet the cultural instance of that same discipline. The fourth is local rationality into global dead ends . A cultural path can be locally rational at every step — each move following the local gradient, a geodesic on the manifold — and still run directly into a singularity. Not every cultural step is rational; coercion, manipulation, and drift push plenty of them. But the ones that are locally rational carry no immunity: a society can follow its own deepest values with perfect fidelity straight into collapse, and — this is the cruel part — feel vindicated the entire way, because collapse-by-your-own-lights still passes your own test. Local rationality is not a safeguard. It is one mechanism of the dead end. The Same Geometry, One Mind Everything so far describes cultures — populations, civilizations, the slow bending of shared terrain. But the geometry is scale-free, and Bach's black-hole metaphor is what it looks like inside a single skull. The gravitational picture is not a second, decorative analogy laid beside the first. It is the manifold's curvature felt from the point of view of the mass falling through it. Capture runs in stages, and naming them is the point of the exercise, because the whole trouble is that from the inside no stage announces itself. It begins as orbit . You hold an ideology at a comfortable distance, one lens among several, and you can still put it down. Nothing here feels dangerous, which is precisely why nothing here resists. Then the pull strengthens. Proximity does the work: confirmation bias, motivated reasoning, and the genuine warmth of in-group approval act together, and each turn inward makes the next one easier and the outward turn harder. The descent accelerates not because the arguments got better but because the field got steeper. Then the event horizon — the threshold past which you no longer evaluate the ideology from outside but reason entirely from within it. Past this line the frame dictates not just which conclusions are permitted but which forms of reasoning are permitted. Disconfirming evidence is not weighed and rejected; it is bent until it complies or it is discarded as bad faith. Competing frameworks are not refuted; they stop being imaginable. You can still speak fluently, argue sharply, marshal evidence — but only along the geodesics the frame allows, and the space of thinkable moves has quietly closed. And then the singularity : absolute certainty, infinite density. Complexity collapses into one totalizing explanation that accounts for everything, including your own doubts, which it recodes as symptoms. Cognitive dissonance is not resolved here; it is annihilated, because the machinery that could host a dissonance has been compressed away. Intellectual humility cannot survive the pressure. Opposition is not defeated. It vanishes from the conceptual field, and its absence feels like clarity. The metaphor earns one more prediction, and it is the sharpest. Black holes warp spacetime across distances far beyond their horizon, and captured ideologies warp discourse the same way — they exert field effects at a distance . A frame that has enough mass bends even its adversaries' language. Opponents find themselves accepting its terms, arguing on its chosen ground, granting its framing of what the question even is, conceding the boundaries of the debate before the debate begins. You do not have to be inside the well to have your trajectory bent by it; you only have to argue nearby.
